utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Nice, you are to cross-examine, but where is the witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: The witness is outside. I saw her outside the door.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mrs. Marinkovic, you remain subject to the declaration that you made.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Mrs. Marinkovic, your work has been contrasted with that of a mere investigator, Barney Kelly, whom you know because you gave a statement to him in April of 2002. Do you have any complaints about the conduct of the interview by Mr. Kelly with you?

utterances.speaker: DANICA MARINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, would you like to ask me specifically so I know what you mean, what you're interested in.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Mrs. Marinkovic, I don't want to put anything to you specifically. I want to know if you have any complaints of any kind about Mr. Kelly's conduct of an interview with you.

utterances.speaker: DANICA MARINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, not the manner in which he conducted the interview. I have nothing to say on that score.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Not only was the statement read over to you in English and B/C/S or Serbian, but you were provided with a copy of the statement yourself in your own language, were you not?

utterances.speaker: DANICA MARINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I never received a copy of that statement of mine, either in Serbian or in English.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: If you didn't receive it I must tell you that one's available, but you have, in any event, no complaints of his conduct. Next thing I want to know, because he's been involved in, for example, the Racak investigation, have you heard anything that you'd like to tell us about that is negative in respect of Mr. Barney Kelly? Feel free to say anything that you've heard that affects his reputation as an investigator.

utterances.speaker: DANICA MARINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's not something I dealt with. It doesn't come within the remit of my work.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I'm giving you a chance. Jonathan Sutch is an OTP investigator who spent several years working in and around Pristina and in Kosovo generally. You may have heard of him. Have you heard anything adverse about Investigator Sutch?

utterances.speaker: DANICA MARINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is the first time I hear of the name. I have never heard the name before, nor do I know the man.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Very well. You see, you as an investigative judge have been contrasted by the accused, at least, with mere investigators of whom you have nothing to complain. Mrs. Marinkovic, you, as we will discover, have been the subject of many complaints, haven't you, in the course of doing your work?

utterances.speaker: DANICA MARINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is not true.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Isn't it? Let's turn to Natasa Kandic. Natasa Kandic is basically the conscience of some Serbs, isn't she?

utterances.speaker: DANICA MARINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know what you mean. Please be more specific.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... things that are true but that it is beyond the courage of others to publish; correct?

utterances.speaker: DANICA MARINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is not something I dealt with. I'm not a journalist, I'm not a publicist, I'm not a representative of some governmental association. I am a judge, a professional, and I only did my job professionally as a judge, so I'm not really interested in comments made by the press; that just isn't part of my job. I'm a professional and I do my job professionally.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: The time of the bombing was a particularly dangerous time for many people, wasn't it, not just because of the bombs but because of what might happen to them at the hands of Serbs; correct?

utterances.speaker: DANICA MARINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not following you. I don't understand the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... Mr. Kelmendi, a famous human rights lawyer who regularly appeared in front of you, was killed, wasn't he, very shortly after the bombing started?

utterances.speaker: DANICA MARINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If you mean the lawyer Bajram Kelmendi, then yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Yes. By whom was he killed? Please tell us.

utterances.speaker: DANICA MARINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: During the time I was in Pristina, the investigation wasn't launched, but a criminal report was filed against perpetrators unknown. So far, we still haven't uncovered the perpetrator, or at least, during the time at least I was in Pristina the perpetrator had not yet been uncovered.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I will return to the Kelmendi death, if I have time in cross-examination, but it must be short. I would like you to consider, if you would just distribute this document before I turn to questions in a chronological order, the sort of things that have been complained about so far as you're concerned. I am afraid this is in English and I haven't obtained or been able to obtain a Serbian version, but you know that Mrs. Kandic heads the Humanitarian Law Centre in Belgrade, doesn't she?

utterances.speaker: DANICA MARINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've heard about that, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: She is herself a Serb.

utterances.speaker: DANICA MARINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: She made observations publicly about the murder of Kosovo Albanian politician Fehmi Agani, didn't she? Didn't she?

utterances.speaker: DANICA MARINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Could you repeat the question? I didn't hear you this time. What were you saying?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... public observations about the murder of Kosovo Albanian politician Fehmi Agani.

utterances.speaker: DANICA MARINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Can you tell me what it was specifically that she said?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Let's look at the article, then, for that. What's more important is the rest of what she was able to complain about. If this can be placed on the overhead projector, please. It's an article of the 8th of March of 2002, a publication of that date. And it says that you, formerly investigating judge of Pristina district court reacted to the Humanitarian Law Centre press release on the murder of Fehmi Agani and accused Natasa Kandic of lying. Did you accuse her of lying?

utterances.speaker: DANICA MARINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Let me tell you this: I'm surprised that you're using as a source of information complaints about my work and that for that you have used Natasa Kandic as a source. For me as an individual, well, I don't know her, she's not interesting as far as I'm concerned. I would like you to tell me specifically in concrete terms the complaints made against my work, whether the parties involved in the proceedings themselves, in the investigation itself, that complained about me, not this source.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... as an overview, and the question to you was capable of an answer. Did you accuse Mrs. Kandic of lying when she pointed to two police officers as responsible for the death of Fehmi Agani?

utterances.speaker: DANICA MARINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Linked to your question, I have concrete proof that I can put before the Trial Chamber. Linked to the Fehmi Agani case, I have nothing to do with that case. I wasn't the investigating judge --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: DANICA MARINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- I didn't compile any on-site report or anything of that kind.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... why did you accuse Mrs. Kandic of lying when she gave an account, a public account, of the killing of an Albanian politician by Serb police officers? Please tell us.

utterances.speaker: DANICA MARINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Because she presented untruths.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: But you --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Nice, sorry to interrupt. I have difficulty following you when you start to speak when the translation continues.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I'm so sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: In which case, why did you accuse her of lying when you knew nothing about it?

utterances.speaker: DANICA MARINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Linked to Fehmi Agani what I know is this: I know a different truth, the truth that was established by the authorised Pristina SUP, and I have proof and evidence of that, and it is the criminal report that was filed by the SUP of Pristina.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Uh-huh. You brought it with you, have you?

utterances.speaker: DANICA MARINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I have.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Thank you. Tell us what it says.

utterances.speaker: DANICA MARINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In this criminal report it says the following: That a criminal report was filed with the district prosecutor Pristina against the perpetrator of a murder, unknown, pursuant to Article 47 of the Criminal Code of Serbia against Fehmi Agani of Pristina. And this criminal report also states the following: On the 6th of May, 1999, at around 1700 hours -- I apologise. I have to put my glasses on. At around 1700 hours in the Batusa district of Kosovo Polje municipality, perpetrators unknown perpetrated the crime of murder under Article 47 of the Criminal Code of Serbia, killing Fehmi Agani of Pristina, who, with three projectiles, was hit in the region of the head from the immediate vicinity. Pursuant to the authority of the investigating judge in Pristina, an on-site investigation was conducted by an employee of the SUP of Pristina on the spot scene of crime next to the main road running from Batusa to Lepjana Lipljan [phoen], and the body was found --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... time is short. We may like to have a look at that document. Is there any particular reason why you brought that document to court, not being involved in it yourself personally?

utterances.speaker: DANICA MARINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Because I assumed that the sole source of your information would unfortunately be Natasa Kandic. If I were in your place as a prosecutor, I would deal a little more with concrete proof and evidence and concrete facts. What she is doing is all hearsay, I-said-she-said. I would like to see what she provided as proof and evidence since she is your sole source of proof, as I see, what evidence she has brought to you about the crimes against Serbs in Kosovo and against other Albanians committed by the Albanian terrorists in Kosovo and Metohija, perhaps that is something that you --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Tell us, please -- you may find you're wrong, but tell us, please, why you're saying that she is a sole source of proof. And actually, while you're about it, let us know how you had any indication in advance at all that I might even refer to Natasa Kandic. How did you know that?

utterances.speaker: DANICA MARINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the press. The press writes about things. This trial is a public trial, and as far as I was able to read from the press, I wasn't able to follow the proceedings in court myself, the press -- it's a public trial, the press wrote about it, and I saw that you used Natasa Kandic as your sole source.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Where do I use Natasa Kandic as my sole source? Let me make it quite plain: What I'm now going to ask you about is whether you have actually got some other source of information or intelligence. Where did you find that - it's quite incorrect - but that we used Natasa Kandic as a sole source? Just help me.

utterances.speaker: DANICA MARINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You know what? This question is superfluous and I would like to appeal to the Trial Chamber to caution Mr. Nice, the Prosecutor, to ask me about my work specifically in concrete terms. I'm a witness here and I'm a judge first and foremost, and I don't want to carry on with this, tiring the Trial Chamber and all the other people here. It's just superfluous.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I'm going to ask you two parts from this document and then we're going to go back and look at things chronologically, and Mrs. Marinkovic although you will have one further reference to Natasa Kandic, we will be looking at many other complaints about you from other sources, have no fear. Could you just help us with these two comments from Natasa Kandic's analysis of your history. In the middle of the page that's on the overhead projector, she says that, "Judge Marinkovic sets herself up as a protector of Serb victims and the Serbian police but her attempts to manipulate public opinion are in vain and that it is known within the police force who killed Fehmi Agani." Do you see yourself as a protector of Serb victims and the Serbian police?

utterances.speaker: DANICA MARINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm -- I just conducted my work professionally and with full conscience.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Then let's look at the foot of this page --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: The ELMO is not just working.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Robinson.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Since the document wasn't provided to the witness in a language the witness understands, it would, I assume, be proper if it were to be read out, the English text, and placed on the ELMO, so that she knows what the text says. It's impossible to work in this way.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Nice. I agree.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: At the moment the ELMO apparently isn't working. While -- to save time, or not waste time, I shall read the bottom paragraph and we'll hope that it will come on display soon.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: This is what has been said by Mrs. Kandic about you: "More and more policemen --"

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Nice, there is a technical problem with the ELMO, so proceed slowly. Read the passage slowly so the witness can hear it.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Certainly.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: "More and more policemen are coming out with what really -- with what really happened in Kosovo. It was from them that I first heard about the murder of Fehmi Agani. I also heard from them that liquidation orders were not given only by police and military commanders. They told me that Danica Marinkovic personally ordered several men in the Ahmeti family to be shot on the 28th of February, 1998, in Likoshan village. Then an investigating judge, she came to conduct an on-site investigation together with Jovica Jovanovic, the deputy district prosecutor, and a team of investigators. There was a pile of bodies outside the Ahmeti house in which some men were still giving signs of life. In the presence of about 30 members of the special anti-terrorist units, Danica Marinkovic allegedly said, 'I'm not taking them. Kill them.' The men were finished off with a Heckler weapon. There was no investigation, and on the 1st of March, 1998, 14 corpses were taken to the Pristina hospital morgue. The investigating judge did not order autopsies to be performed, and after they were identified, the bodies were claimed by relatives." Now, can you think of any reason why policemen should give such an account to Natasa Kandic, please?

utterances.speaker: DANICA MARINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Give me the names of those policemen. When did they tell her that?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I'm asking you, can you think of any reason why policemen should give that account to her?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I have to say, Mr. Nice, I think the witness's question's a perfectly fair one to you in the circumstances. This is a very grave allegation you're making against the witness here, and to make it on the basis of a press report alone at the moment, and I accept that may not be your only basis, seems a pretty thin one.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I quite understand that.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Nevertheless, in light --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone Mr. Nice, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And in light of the breadth of this witness's evidence on topics germane to this Trial Chamber, I'm concerned with her reputation and I want only an answer to the question can she think of any -- can she give us any reason why police officers should have said such things about her to Natasa Kandic?

utterances.speaker: DANICA MARINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You know what, I really can't answer that question until you give me the names of the policemen and when they made the statement and where. I'm interested in the names and the time. If it was in 1998, for example, why is that just being mentioned in 2002?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Very well. If I can, I'll come back to that later this morning before I finish, because I want to go back now in time --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Nice, it is such a grave allegation to make against the judge. I would say that if you have the evidence to support it, you should bring it in rebuttal.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: If I'm able to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: It's a very grave allegation.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: If I'm able to, I will. At the moment I'm dealing with her reputation. I'm contrasting her reputation with those of others. I've given her every opportunity to make observations about others, and the Chamber will see more material coming, not from Natasa Kandic, about this witness. With Your Honours' leave, may I go to the start of matters chronologically, and I'm only going to be able to deal with some of the topics that have been covered.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Can you help me, please --

utterances.speaker: DANICA MARINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: May I be allowed to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Very briefly.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] -- to tell the Trial Chamber, if I might be allowed to do so. I don't know where the place is, nor was I ever there. I just would like the Trial Chamber to bear that in mind. As to the rest, I'll leave it up to Mr. Nice to give me the concrete facts; the names and the time. The names of the policemen who gave that statement, where, on what premises, and why they waited from 1998 until the year 2002. But I'd just like to apprise the Chamber of the fact that I was never there, in the place he mentioned.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I want to go back no further than 1987, and then for one point only. Can you help us, please, with your husband's first name.

utterances.speaker: DANICA MARINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know why that is important --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: You have to answer --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] -- for my testimony here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: You have to answer the question. We will see the purpose of the question.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Stevan.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And he was a friend of and, for a time at least, an associate of the man Solevic, who was an activist in Kosovo. Am I not correct?

utterances.speaker: DANICA MARINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I really don't know. In 1987, that was a long time ago. I don't know who his friends were at the time. I wasn't interested.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Following the accused's famous Kosovo Polje speech "You will not be beaten" where Solevic features on the evidence before this Tribunal, various demonstrations were organised, including, of course, the yoghurt Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. revolution, which led to the downfall or the change in the autonomy of Vojvodina. Your husband was one of the group of men, including Solevic and others, who went around organising those revolution -- those activities. Am I not right?

utterances.speaker: DANICA MARINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: What does that have to do with me?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Please answer the question. Am I not right?

utterances.speaker: DANICA MARINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You know what? In 1987 so many things happened that I cannot remember everything. I know that the Serbs from Kosovo and Metohija raised their voice because they were second-rate citizens in Kosovo and Metohija, so they asked for their rights to be respected; their human rights, their rights to work, to freedom of movement, and that is why they were involved in these manifestations. I don't know the details. I was never involved in politics. I was never a member of any party. I've been a professional judge since 1984, ever since I was first appointed judge. I'm a judge until the present day. I was never interested in these details.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Nevertheless, I'll give you one last opportunity, please, answer the question: Was your husband one of those in 1988, possibly into 1989, I don't know, was politically very active in support of this accused and in the way I've suggested, going around to other places to be involved in demonstrations?

utterances.speaker: DANICA MARINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If you're so interested in his activity, you can call him and he can explain it to you in greater detail. I don't know. It is true that he is one of the Serbs out of all the Serbs in Kosovo and Metohija who were striving for their rights, because at that time they were second-rate citizens in Kosovo and Metohija.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mrs. Marinkovic, at the time referred to by Mr. Nice, were you living in an ordinary domestic relationship with your husband?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: You may be right when you say, What's the point of the questions? That's for us to judge in due course. But I have to say that your answers at the moment strike me on this subject as very evasive. You're a very experienced judge. Can we not just get straight to the issues that you ought to be aware of and deal with them and then we'll sort out in due course what weight to give to these answers.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May I say the following: I do not understand at all why there is so much insistence on my husband's activities. I came here to testify as a judge about my work and about the cases that I worked on. As for my family life and my husband's life, that is not relevant to the Trial Chamber and to the subject of my testimony. I am not being evasive about what he has been doing. He did take part with the other Serbs in those demonstrations so that Serbs would get the status that they deserve in Kosovo and Metohija. That's no secret. Everybody knew that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you. Thank you, Mrs. Marinkovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Can I say, the trouble is we don't know that. We have to get the information by answers to questions that are put.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: You see, so that it's quite clear now that you've given that last answer, Mrs. Marinkovic, I am going to suggest that from the end of the 1980s you were yourself political and a supporter of this accused and of Serbs as against non-Serbs, and I'm now going to explore why, but that's the suggestion and that's why I've asked you the question. Do you follow?

utterances.speaker: DANICA MARINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I do not follow. I do not understand this question.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Can we turn to your exhibit, tab 4.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: The Court will recall that a large number of exhibits were produced as records of trials. I'm only going to deal, and briefly, with one of them because I want to focus my attention on Racak, of course, but I'm going to deal with things chronologically. I want us to look first of all at tab 4. If the witness could have the volumes that are provided for the witness open at the B/C/S -- the Serbian version, if she would prefer it, of tab 4.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Now, tab 24 is a trial -- sorry, tab 4 was a trial for which you were the investigating judge; correct? And it was known as the police trial.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May I just put a question now? Can I now answer these questions since they were not part of my examination-in-chief by the Defence? In relation to this particular judgement, I did not give any answers to questions put by the Defence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, well the questions may nonetheless be put to you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Now --

utterances.speaker: DANICA MARINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- I carried out the investigation against these persons against whom the indictment was brought in 1995.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Before we look at the record and some other documents in relation to this trial, I want you to look at another exhibit.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Your Honour, it's -- and if the Court would -- it's a document which comes in, at the moment, two parts. There's part -- let me explain it. It's easier. I'll ask the Court first to go to the Serbian version, the last page of the document, where it will see what looks like and indeed is a petition. If you turn to the Serbian version. We have had some trouble getting this and a translation of any part of it. And the Court -- if it's on the overhead projector, Mr. Prendergast, the Serbian version on. I gather we're still not having success with the overhead projector. The Court will see an extract of a petition, and above it on the right it will see nine numbered points. This petition is extracted in this form from one newspaper which we do not have a translation because it's only been obtained recently. However, if the Chamber turns to the English version document, which comes from another newspaper, and goes to the second page, it will see the nine numbered points, and it's only the nine numbered points in which I'm interested.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: But if you, Mrs. Marinkovic, would be good enough, please, to look at the Serb version of the extract of the petition, was this a petition with which you were familiar?

utterances.speaker: DANICA MARINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: First of all, I do not see the date here when this was published and what newspaper actually carried this. At least, it's not here in the Serbian. I don't know what this petition has to do with my work on the case.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: What we have at the foot --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Do you not see the right bottom of the page?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: It's the Nin newspaper for the 21st of October, Trafalgar Day, of 199--

utterances.speaker: DANICA MARINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Oh, it's down here, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Now, this petition, which has many names, to some degree being passed secretly from hand to hand to be signed, were you aware of it?

utterances.speaker: DANICA MARINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is 1994. I cannot recall this petition.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Do you recall whether you or whether, to your knowledge, your husband signed this petition?

utterances.speaker: DANICA MARINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: In which case I'll withdraw that because I can't ask the witness to produce it. But I'm going to suggest to you that towards the end of 1994, dissatisfaction of the state of political affairs under the accused's leadership at that time led to demands by Serbs for action and that your trial of the policemen, tab 4, was in part a response to Serb nationalist demands. That's what I'm suggesting.

utterances.speaker: DANICA MARINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Do you have a question in relation to my work on that case?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: That's the question. I'm suggesting to you that this case, this quite well-known policemen case, or police case, was in part a response to the dissatisfaction of Serbs with the political activity of this accused at that time and the governments generally? Yes?

utterances.speaker: DANICA MARINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's not correct. That assertion of yours is not correct. The petition has nothing to do with the case that I worked on. This group that is mentioned here in 1995, after my investigation, an indictment was issued, a first instance judgement was passed. The Supreme Court of Serbia confirmed the judgement, and I don't see what legal proceedings that came to a valid conclusion have -- how they can have something to do with a newspaper article and petition in 1994. Can you put specific questions to me about my work? I'm not interested in politics. I'm a professional judge. I was elected judge in 1984, at the time when Mr. Milosevic was not in power. And I worked, and I work today. I have been working until this very day when Mr. Milosevic is not in power, and I think it would only be fair to put questions to me as to a professional judge, not putting to me some kind of information from newspapers. I'm not interested in that. I stand by my cases and my work.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mrs. Marinkovic. I think you have answered the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: You see, tab 4, although you weren't asked any questions about it, it was in fact one of many exhibits introduced through you right at the end of the last session, and it's about that that I want to ask you a few questions. You know, or you know of and remember, a lawyer called Fazli Balaj, who represented some six, I think, defendants in this case; correct?

utterances.speaker: DANICA MARINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot remember. I carried out the investigation in 1994. I had 89 accused persons, 89 indictees. Every one of them had at least two or three lawyers. So now to remember from 1994 who defended who is something I cannot remember. In the first instance judgement, which has also been tendered into evidence, there is an exact reference to who the indictees were and who the accused persons were and who the lawyers were. There were 89 indictees involved, and after the investigation was completed, when the prosecutor received these materials, the prosecutor decided not to prosecute 16 persons -- rather, 17 persons, because the ultimate number of indictees was 72, not 89.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mrs. Marinkovic. Proceed, Mr. Nice.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: You've given an account of how you're a responsible and professional judge, and we're just going to look at little bits of this one trial. You say you don't remember the particular lawyer. Is it right, so that we can understand how the system worked, that lawyers were not allowed contact with their clients in the early stages of their detentions?

utterances.speaker: DANICA MARINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's not correct. Lawyers were given permission to see the detainees whenever they wanted to. I signed these permits, and these permits do exist in the district prison. These records are kept. Every lawyer had that right and was given the possibility to contact his clients.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: The second thing I'm going to suggest to you is that it was not uncommon, it may have been very common, for accused persons to be beaten and even tortured in prison while they were detained at your order and therefore in your charge. Is that true?

utterances.speaker: DANICA MARINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In relation to that, tell me, what kind of evidence do you have? This is the first time I hear of this. I'm not aware of that. As for the cases that I investigated, this is the first time I hear of any such thing. Give me a specific name.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... shall we? We'll just have a look at one, there may be several documents, but here is a document dated the 27th of February, 1995. Maybe this slipped your memory, because this, you see, is a complaint by the defending lawyer, Fazli Balaj, and he says it's his fifth complaint, and there's a summary. For want of time it hasn't been possible, but you've got the full original. He summarises earlier complaints and sets out how on the 24th of February he visited his defendants in the district gaol and how his defendant Isak Aliu "told me that he was taken out for interrogation on the 17th, 21st and 22nd of February, subject to physical torture, beaten on his arms and back and told he would examined on the 23rd of February." The complaint went on to say there are vivid injuries on his body, and he requests -- the lawyer requested that Isak Aliu be sent for medical examination, and he asked you to interfere with the organs of state to stop them torturing him, because he was under your competencies and not the under the competencies of the state security. He explained to you that his client had been threatened that his family would be killed, and he said at the end, "As a defending lawyer, I cannot understand why the accused get interrogated by the members of state security." Do you not remember that complaint being made? Is this so routine that you don't remember it?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Robinson.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is a highly improper question. Mr. Nice says does that happen that often that she can't remember these things? Although Mrs. Marinkovic said this is the first time that she heard of any time -- of any kind of torture of detainees?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: I think the question was, "Is this so routine that you don't remember it?" Let the witness answer the question.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is beyond anything I can imagine. It defies belief. They are trying to make excuses for themselves, the Defence lawyers. I can just say that every detainee was subjected to a medical examination whenever Defence attorneys asked for that to be done. In prison, there was a prison doctor who examined the detainees, and this was in line with the Code of Conduct in prison. Whenever I had any such motion from any Defence counsel, I always issued instructions to have medical examinations carried out and to establish whether there were any injuries. If Mr. Nice got this, then he should have gotten all the documents; my instructions given to the prison administration and so on. So this doesn't mean anything to me if I cannot see the rest of the evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: The same complaint was made by the lawyer. He pressed on. If we have a look at perhaps 26, he sent the complaint to the minister of interior. Did the minister of the interior contact you about this complaint? Coming up. Do you remember the complaint being processed through the minister?

utterances.speaker: DANICA MARINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. This is the first time I see this. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: In which case let's look at the next exhibit as well -- next document as well. Number 27, please. The same lawyer --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: These -- well --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Nice, these two documents you've given us so far are the same date.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: So it does look as though the complaint was made to the minister the same day --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Same day, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: -- as it was addressed to the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And the next one comes the day after, in fact, and it's to the chairman of the local court, the examining magistrate, and others.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Look at this document, please, which is sent to many people, apparently, and complains about you not having done anything. It so far says "have so far done anything."

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I expect that's a translation error, Your Honour, and that if we read from the original, it's only recently before me, it will read as having done nothing because otherwise the context isn't realistic.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: See, I must suggest to you, Mrs. Marinkovic, the reality of the trials you've been describing to this Court is radically different from the sort of process with which this Court may itself be familiar, and that prisoners were maltreated. Is that not right?

utterances.speaker: DANICA MARINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is what you say. That is not my view. Since you found all of these documents, you should have also come up with the documents that the court issued. This is only documents provided by the Defence counsel and that suits you, but you don't have any of the documents that the court issued, the minister, the judges, et cetera. This is one-sided. Provide the documents in their entirety and then let us discuss them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mrs. Marinkovic, can you assist us by telling us your recollection of what happened when these communications were received?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Specifically as regards these documents, I cannot say anything, but I can say how I worked on every case. Whenever I would receive such a submission, I would always act upon it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Can I -- can I interrupt you? That suggests -- you see, I know that Mr. Milosevic took exception to the question Mr. Nice asked about it being routine, but what you're saying at the moment suggests that you routinely got complaints about accused people being beaten up and having to be sent for medical attention. Now, is that what you're saying?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, no.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: If you're not saying that, then surely you would remember this case.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May I say the following: First of all, this is not correct. Detainees after I hear them and after I pass a decision on conducting investigation, they are sent to the district prison, and then no one can torture them nor did anyone ever torture anybody. I can tell you that often we had --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Does it then follow that you're saying this is falsified?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, I'm not saying that, but I can tell you that lawyers wrote all sorts of things, whatever suited them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, that is what you're saying then, that it's falsified. No?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Well, I don't know whether it's falsified. There is a seal attesting to the fact that it was received. However, Mr. Nice should have submitted the documents in their entirety, not only the submission made by the Defence counsel. May I say another thing. Often we had delegations from the International Red Cross coming to visit the institutions of our prisons. I gave them permission to do that, they came often, and the detainees and prisoners had the opportunity of talking to them, voicing their objections, if any. In my investigations, this kind of thing never happened --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone for Mr. Nice, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I'll conclude, at least for the time being but probably altogether with this topic, with two more issues. First, perhaps you'd be good enough to look at some documents that have an earlier date. 22nd and thereabouts of December, 1994.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: There is a collection, Your Honour, of I think three, four -- ten medical records.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: If you'd like to look at the first one, and we can all go through them rapidly together. If you'd be good enough to look, please, at the foot of the page, there's a stamp. Can you tell us what the stamp is? Please? The stamp of the Institute of Forensic Medicine in Pristina?

utterances.speaker: DANICA MARINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The institute. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And we can see that the signatures include that of the forthcoming witness, Dr. Dobricanin. If we look at the body of this report, it says at the request of the court, the medical board carried out an examination of Alija Isak from Urosevac, and then it says, 2, the skin of the palm of the hand livid greenish; left palm area including the lower part of the forearm, the skin is livid greenish and yellowish in colour, sub-skin is suffused with blood. Left thigh purple, greenish, yellowish. Ankle peeled off, bare skin dry, brown-red in colour. Opinion: Haematomas inflicted by heavy blow from blunt heavy mechanical implement. Described as minor injury. Did you receive that report? Did you? As the judge caring for the security of these men? These are all defendants in the police case.

utterances.speaker: DANICA MARINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, this is proof that I acted pursuant to the law. I gave an order for examination so that with this individual it could be established what happened. Now, as the lawyer set it out in his motion, it's not correctly set out. It says here that it was a -- not light bodily harm with a blow from a blunt instrument. Now, where he received that blow from, who inflicted the blow, and things like that were not established.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: The problem with that I think may be the date, because this report predates the complaint we've been looking at already. So it's not clear at the moment what the relationship is.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: But the point is, Mrs. Marinkovic, that if we look at all these, and we don't have time to go through them in detail -- well, let's ask the question: Did you receive reports of this kind? Yes or no.

utterances.speaker: DANICA MARINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The report is addressed to me, the investigating judge, so I'm sure that this document exists in the case files.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And therefore - we can look at all of them but at the moment I'm not going to take the time to do that - you have received reports suggesting that prisoners in detention at your instruction were showing signs of being hit by a blunt object or objects. You then subsequently received complaints from the lawyers sent to ministers and others about really serious injury being committed to his clients. Does that trouble you?

utterances.speaker: DANICA MARINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Those are your observations and conclusions. I cannot comment. Give me a specific question and I'll be happy to answer it.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I have given you a specific question. You've told us about your practices. You've confirmed that medical reports of this kind would be received by you. The complaints made by the lawyer were addressed to you and to all other organs from which it is reasonable to suppose that you might have heard, I would suggest, and my very specific question to you, Mrs. Marinkovic, is: Did this worry, trouble you?

utterances.speaker: DANICA MARINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You know what? In -- that was 1994. We're 2006 [as interpreted] now. So much time has gone by that I can't comment on events that happened at that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Well, you're going to comment on events that happened in 1999. Where is the cut-off point from your memory, please? 1999, yes; 1994, no? What is it?

utterances.speaker: DANICA MARINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Nice, I should like to remind you that I am a witness here, but I'm also a judge. So have a little respect towards my position.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I'm showing you appropriate respect. You have given wide-ranging evidence when you were last here on what did and did not happen without any reference, so far as I can immediately recall, to problems with recollection. You were asked to produce, and although you may not have understood the technicalities of it, you produced exhibits 4 through to 44, being records of your trials. I'm asking you questions about one of them and I'm providing you with contemporaneous documents. May we take it that even with contemporaneous documents, you have no recollection and cannot help us with events in 1994?

utterances.speaker: DANICA MARINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I handed over the court files from which you can see and read everything that went on. Now, as to the details of it all, I cannot recount them again here now, and it would be a better thing if you had the complete set of case files to study and to see what they contain, because I don't want to speak from my memory now and answer what suits you best.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Nice, I'm not sure that I understand your purpose in this line of cross-examination. The prisoners are in detention. You say that they are subject to her care. They're beaten. She has said that when she receives reports that they're beaten, she orders an examination of them. Are you also suggesting that she should have taken measures to prevent their being beaten?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: She should have taken measures to prevent them being beaten. She should have taken more measures to have them examined continuously, and all sorts of other things, yes. She didn't do those things is my suggestion to her.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: And that's within her jurisdiction?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Yes. And also fundamentally that the regime in which she was operating was one in which prisoners were beaten. Certainly in political cases of this kind.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I would like just to make one comment about the last answer that the judge gave. You're very critical of Mr. Nice for not presenting what you describe as all the case papers, but this question arises -- or these questions arise because you have produced what purport to be the case papers in relation to this particular case, and now you're not able to give answers to questions which are directed to the case.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You know what? They're the details of the case. I can't remember all the details now, but within the frameworks of my competencies and authority, I did take steps. And these are not political cases, as Mr. Nice claims. Here we had a crime, and they are being accused of association in order to commit hostile activity. That is a crime which comes under the Criminal Code of Yugoslavia and is one of the crimes stipulated there. And they weren't interrogated several times, as Mr. Nice claims. They came up before me as investigating judge once with their defence, and then we continued to collect evidence. We had nothing more to do with them. Everything else, the position of detainees is taken over by the prison authorities and it is they who are responsible after that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Just let me follow that. I think that's the point I was getting at, Mr. Nice. If a prisoner is beaten and it's brought to the attention of the judge, the judge can take steps to see that the person is examined by a doctor.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: But the actual prevention of the beating, I imagine the judge could also issue an order for the prison authorities to ensure that no beating -- no more beatings take place.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: The -- the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: But beyond that, it's not clear to me what the judge is to do.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I should have made one point clear. I think the judge will be able to confirm this.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: The examination on the 22nd of December, 1994, was about a month after the arrest and the initial request, wasn't it, because apart from the written complaints here, the initial request of the lawyer had been about a month before, and you let a month pass so that the injuries would fade. Isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: DANICA MARINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. You have the documents. But what I want to say is this: The person in question, before they were escorted to prison, was interviewed about me in the presence of their Defence counsel and an interpreter. And if they had any complaints, any remarks to make with respect to his position in the pre-trial stage, he could have told me that in person. Then I could have taken note of it by way of minutes and then taken steps to ensure a medical examination. But when I interviewed him, he never made any complaints as to his status and position. And always when I wrote down the minutes and took notes if I saw any visible signs of injury, particularly if the person in question complained to me that he had sustained injuries and if I can see with my own eyes visible injuries on his face such as bruises and so on, then this is taken note of. And the Defence counsel who is present during the interview asks that this be recorded in the minutes. All this is done in the presence of a prosecutor, the defence counsel, and the interpreter, as I said. So you can't hide things of that kind. Now where he sustained those injuries, I really don't know. I gave an order for a medical examination to be conducted and the forensic experts noted that there was bodily injury. That is where my authority ends. So there was no grievous bodily harm which required further medical treatment. Now, how these injuries were inflicted, in what way, that's not up to me. It wasn't up to me to investigate that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mrs. Marinkovic, I'm interested in the charges the accused were accused of. You said they were accused of association in order to commit hostile activity. Can one be prosecuted only because of the association without doing -- committing actual crimes?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This group mentioned in this case, they are being accused of the crime of association in order to commit hostile activity with the goal of violent secession of part of Serbia or Yugoslavia, the creation of an independent state, and possibly conjoining with Albania. Now, through this association they had planned and organised -- they first of all made an association, then they trained in Albania, and then illegally brought in weapons and then prepared and organised all these activities which were geared towards the forceful violent secession of part of Serbia and Yugoslavia and the creation of an independent state. Those are all elements which comprise and represent a crime pursuant to Article 136 of -- under the heading of association in order to engage in hostile activities. So this was a large group of people who had associated on the basis of a prior agreement, and their aim was forcibly to cut off -- to become separate from Serbia. This is what we call the illegal MUP, as it's referred to.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Yes. This is the parallel institutions which had been in existence from 1991 and there came a time when it decided to prosecute; right?

utterances.speaker: DANICA MARINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Can we look at another document, which is a report of the Humanitarian Law Centre, a contemporaneous report of 1995. Again it's in English, and I'm only going to read two short passages and ask for your comments on it before I move on.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And if the Court would like to turn to -- seeing that it's a February 1995 report by Humanitarian Law Centre, director Natasa Kandic, and if would like to go to page 23. I am sorry, but it doesn't exist at present, in any event, in Serbian.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: But here's a summary that this non-governmental organisation provided of the trial, or comment on it in any event. Halfway down the left-hand side of the page. Little -- there you go. A bit further. By the -- thank you very much. "By the end of 1994, criminal proceedings had begun against officials and members of the union of former Kosovo policemen who were accused of belonging to a Kosovo-Albanian parapolice force. "The courts have treated membership in any association of Kosovo Albanians, activism in support of specific political opinion, the distribution of leaflets or flyers, the setting up of committees attached to the LDK political party, the formation of professional and other civic organisations which neither use nor advocate violence, the collection of material on human rights violations, and even the making of lists of men between the ages of 16 and 90, all as preparatory for acts under 136 of the Yugoslav Criminal Code, punishable under Articles 116." Now, is this magazine's analysis of the criminal proceedings taken against expressly non-violent acts accurate? Mrs. Marinkovic, is it accurate that proceedings were taken against activities that were all themselves non-violent?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As Mr. Nice is using a report dated 1995 and provided by Natasa Kandic, if the Trial Chamber allows me, I would like to quote individual passages of the judgement and indictment so that it can become clear to the Trial Chamber what was afoot, what this was all about, and then the Trial Chamber can rule whether the report by Natasa Kandic is correct and exact or whether it is arbitrary and not based on proof and evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Before we do that, can you tell me what Article 136 of the Yugoslav Criminal Code says? These are the acts that were preparatory to Article 136 of the Yugoslav Criminal Code, so it's important to know what that provision says.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I can read out to you the text of the Criminal Code, the law.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Well, just -- if you can just give us a summary of what it says. If it's very long, then just give us a summary.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Anybody engaging in associations, bands, or other ganging up in order to perpetrate crimes pursuant to Article -- anybody engaging in conspiracy, gangs, bands, or groups in order to perform crimes under Article 114 to 119 and Articles 120 to 123 and Articles 125 to 127 and Article 132 of this Criminal Code will receive a prison term ranging between one to ten years. Now, here in connection with this group we relate it to Article 136 and 170 -- 116 of the same Criminal Code, which says jeopardising the territorial integrity, anybody attempting by use of force or other counter-constitutional means to cut off any part of the SFRY territory or to conjoin it to another state will be punished by a prison term of no less than five years.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Nice, speaking for myself, I don't find this line of cross-examination very productive, very helpful.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: As Your Honour pleases.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: You're trying to show that the judge is biased, that she was politically motivated, that she's partial to the accused. These are legal issues that you're dealing with, and there will always be an explanation as to why these people were charged under Article 136.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Your Honour, that may be, but the environment in which this witness was operating and the facts of no doubt all the cases, if I had a chance to deal with -- time to deal with them all, might be of interest. I've focused on one, tab 4, out of whatever it is, 40 files, and I would seek leave -- not leave. I would seek to be able to -- certainly to have the witness answer my last question which comes from the Spotlight publication, and I was going to ask her to comment on some factual points that are made on the following page, page 24, and the Chamber can see the points on the right-hand column, because there is the clear suggestion that this is a woman and judge of utmost integrity. That is not something -- professional integrity. It's not something I can accept, and it's therefore my duty to lay the material to her to some degree for her to deal with. My intention, having dealt with this and our position on the witness, is to move to Racak as soon as I can.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I hope this isn't an unfair characterisation of what we've achieved in an hour and 20 minutes this morning, but have we not simply established only that there was one accused person who may have made complaints about subsequent beating up which were not investigated, and that's hanging -- that's hanging in the air? And beyond that, what have we actually established this morning?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, things do move slowly, and it's not entirely possible to move them any more swiftly, but if the Court would be good enough to go with me to page 24 of this document. No, Your Honour, I hope we are establishing rather more than that because it's necessary for us to have a -- it maybe desirable for us to have an understanding of the realities of the system that applied at the time. Now, if the witness is not going to accept my characterisation of it, and I put it to her in general terms at the beginning, the process of establishing it via contemporaneous and other material is never going to be quick, but I can only do my best.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: You see, if we look at page 24, dealing with the same investigation, on the left-hand column we have this, that "Between November the 17th and December the 5th more than 200 members of the Union of Former Kosovo Province Policemen were arrested." I think that's true, isn't it, Mrs. Marinkovic?

utterances.speaker: DANICA MARINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, it is not true. Now, I don't know the probative value for the Trial Chamber, whether they have the court files, whether it is the court files and all the rest of it or is it what -- the writings of Natasa Kandic. Here we have a judgement of the Supreme Court of Serbia brought in 1999 which confirms the judgement of the first instance. And I think it is absolutely out of order for me to have to comment on Natasa Kandic's writings. I don't think she is worthy of us spending so much time on her.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: We'll determine that, Mrs. Marinkovic, if you don't mind.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: She, or at any event the magazine published by her organisation, reports the death in custody of somebody called Ismail Raka. I must suggest to you that he was badly treated and beaten before, as it was said here, jumping out of a window. Is that true?

utterances.speaker: DANICA MARINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't understand. I don't know who you're talking about. Who are you referring to? May I have the name? The name, the evidence and so on; when, where, what.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: The person Ismail Raka. He died in custody. Do you not remember that?

utterances.speaker: DANICA MARINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: In December of 1994. You really don't remember the death in custody of one of your accused?

utterances.speaker: DANICA MARINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: From this group, you say.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Yes. That's what I'm asking you about.

utterances.speaker: DANICA MARINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: What number is he in the indictment?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Your Honour, I -- I think I'm just going to cut it and move on. Not because I --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Robinson.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: -- we don't have time.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Asking questions of this kind of Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. this witness, a witness who doesn't know the language from which the quotes come, is completely improper. The whole passage or paragraph should be read out, at least. If the witness were able to read in this language she would be able to read it out. Regardless of whether what is stated is correct or is not correct, she would be able to read it. Now you're confronting court files with somebody's writings. It says very clearly here that one of the detainees died while he was in prison and that the Tanjug news agency published a statement made by the Pristina district court or the person representing it who proclaimed his death, and in keeping with that statement he says that Raka jumped from the fifth floor of the police station and that was how he died. That's what it says here. Now, I don't know -- I have no way knowing whether that is correct or not, but it is elementary good behaviour to read it out to Mrs. Marinkovic, at least a portion of the text which is written in a language she doesn't understand. Then perhaps she would remember whether it happened or not.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you for reading it out, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I want to move on, if I may, to Racak, Mrs. Marinkovic. We're going to have a look at what you saw and what you didn't see. First of all, I'd just like to confirm that included in the elements important to your conclusion that there had been no massacre but that there was a battle, included in the important elements was the fact that the victims all were wearing the same belts; is that right? Similar trousers and the same belts. Do you remember telling us that?

utterances.speaker: DANICA MARINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: First of all, if you were following my testimony over the previous days, I said that I as the investigating judge make no conclusions. I as an investigating judge just collect evidence. So that your conclusion as stated by you is incorrect. I don't make the conclusions. The conclusions are made by the prosecutor once I send in all the evidence that I have collected and amassed; on the spot, scene of crime, and subsequently. Now ask me a specific question without any conclusions, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: You sent in as part of the evidence that you found that all the victims were wearing the same belts. Was that part of your report on the evidence that you found?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. They were wearing leather belts. Most of those victims. Whether each and every one I can't say for sure, but most of them were wearing the same leather belts.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And did you think there was some significance in that?

utterances.speaker: DANICA MARINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I took note of that and wrote it down, recorded it. Whether it was significant or not was up to the prosecutor to decide. So it was my duty to observe all these things, to record them, and within the framework of all the evidence found at the scene of crime, or on-site, it was up to the prosecutor to decide.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Because apart from making observations of the bodies and the weaponry that was found, you made no inquiry of any local resident, did you?

utterances.speaker: DANICA MARINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: You made no inquiry of the local military forces to deal with the suggestion that the military had been involved?

utterances.speaker: DANICA MARINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't have the authority to interview or interrogate the army, because that didn't come under my remit. And I didn't see any military forces or military vehicles in the area. The army wasn't present from the 15th to the 18th when I tried to enter Racak. There were no soldiers round about, no military forces --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: You made no inquiry --

utterances.speaker: DANICA MARINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- see any.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... any survivor?

utterances.speaker: DANICA MARINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, because I didn't know who was in the village, whether there were any survivors at all. I didn't know their names.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And fundamentally, and perhaps the last question if the Court's about to adjourn, fundamentally in an incident which is being characterised, if not by you by the accused, as a conflict rather than a massacre, you made no inquiry of who is presumed to be the other party to the conflict, namely the police, did you?

utterances.speaker: DANICA MARINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was not within my competence and authority, because I didn't know who had taken part in the conflict. I didn't know that.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: If the conflict, if it was a conflict between the police acting lawfully and the KLA acting unlawfully, we don't actually have an account in this investigation, unless I've missed it, of what the lawfully acting police say occurred, do we?

utterances.speaker: DANICA MARINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It came under the authority and competence of the prosecutor to establish and decide if he deemed necessary. And I have his Official Note from Racak, for example. I can write -- I can read out what the prosecutor -- what steps he took after I had sent in my papers and records based on Racak.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Nice, let us take the break now.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Certainly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: And when we return, perhaps the witness can tell us of whom did she make any inquiries in relation to her investigation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: And --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Nice, I'm reminded to ask you to deal with the exhibits individually.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Certainly, yes. Yes. I'll deal with them individually. I rather suspect their admissibility might in certain cases be judged one in relation to another, but I'll review it certainly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: We will adjourn for 20 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Nice.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Two things outstanding. One is whether the exhibits should be dealt with now or whether in the particular circumstances of this witness it might be better to deal with them all comprehensively at the end. I only say that because I realise that, for example, the documents coming from Natasa Kandic may require special consideration although they seem to me are documents published about this witness of which she appears to be aware.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: They can be dealt with at the end.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Then Your Honour's outstanding question of the witness was as to whom she did make inquiries of in relation to her investigation.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Mrs. Marinkovic, of whom did you make inquiries in your investigation?

utterances.speaker: DANICA MARINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In relation to Racak, I carried out an on-site investigation. So that is one part of the investigation process. In relation to that on-site investigation, I took other investigative activities on the basis of which I could act and where I had authority to do so. In that stage, I could not interview any one of the witnesses because I needed a request for that from the authorised public prosecutor. On site I cannot interview anyone until I have a request submitted by the prosecutor. The only thing I can do is carry out an on-site investigation and record my immediate observations and include the evidence that I find on the spot. This is in accordance with the law on criminal procedure. This was very important for me. After I carried out the investigation, after I found the bodies, the weapons, another investigative activity that I ordered was post-mortems of the bodies found in Racak so that cause of death could be established. Another investigative activity --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mrs. Marinkovic, let me understand you clearly. You're saying that according to your procedure, you carry out an on-site investigation, and that is exclusively confined to your observations to what you saw. You report what you saw. You're not allowed to interview witnesses.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: You see, without interviewing witnesses, it's impossible to draw very satisfactory conclusions, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: DANICA MARINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In relation to the on-site investigation, I can establish only what I myself found on site. That is what I record, but no conclusions are made. It is premature to make any conclusions.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: DANICA MARINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Walker's conclusions were premature. Tell me --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: We're not talking about Mr. Walker at the moment. You see, another Defence witness, Mr. Adam, when asked questions by Mr. Saxon about the type of comprehensive investigation that would be required for Racak agreed that talking to people like the police and armed units would be a sensible thing to do. Would you disagree with Mr. Adam on that, that it would be sensible to deal with the police, to talk with the police and the armed units?

utterances.speaker: DANICA MARINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Again, I repeat, according to the law on criminal procedure --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: We've heard that. We're concerned with inquiries or investigations that lead to conclusions, because I'm going to suggest that's exactly why you're here. Another thing or another summarising part of Mr. Adam's evidence was that an investigation that made no attempt to speak to survivors or the -- or the involved other party, the police, would be deficient. He accepted that. Do you accept that an inquiry that made no investigation of survivors or the police would be deficient?

utterances.speaker: DANICA MARINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You see, investigation is part of criminal procedure. On-site investigation is just one investigation activity. After that particular investigative activity, the process continues. The prosecutor, if he deems necessary, can submit a request to the investigating judge, asking him or her to carry out at that stage -- could you please hear me out. Can I explain an answer. You don't know our law on criminal procedure sufficiently, after all, so please be patient and let me explain. That is why I am here as a witness, a judge who is a witness, in order to clarify these matters. If the prosecutor believes that after the investigation of Racak is complete and on the basis of all the evidence that I gave him, if he wants me to carry out additional investigative activity, he then submits a request stating what witnesses I should hear and with regard to what situations. In respect of Racak, everything I did in connection with the investigation I submitted to the prosecutor. The prosecutor compiled an Official Note.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... we are getting --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Could I -- I've been waiting to say something about this.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mrs. Marinkovic, I think Mr. Nice knows perfectly well what your system is and that you do him a disservice by suggesting otherwise. He asked a question about -- which would require an opinion from a very experienced judge. Now, are you saying that because you're not a prosecutor you're not prepared to give that question -- give an answer to that question, or are you simply avoiding answering the question?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. I am prepared to answer every specific question within my authority and knowledge as an investigative judge, but let the Prosecutor be specific. Let him put specific questions to me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, I have to say that it seems to me a very obvious question to ask a person experienced in investigation whether when investigating an incident that resulted in a significant number of deaths but there were survivors whether the investigation could possibly be regarded as complete without an attempt being made to speak to the survivors.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Again, I am telling you in relation to Racak, no investigation was carried out. Only one particular investigative activity was carried out, namely the on-site investigation. Then the prosecutor, when receiving evidence related to the on-site investigation and the complete evidence gathered in Racak, then the prosecutor took further steps that he deemed necessary. In relation to Racak, he gave his own report as a prosecutor, and then written orders to the SUP in Pristina what action the SUP should take in relation to that. I was not in charge. I was not authorised to act in that section without express -- without an express request from the prosecutor.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Are you aware of the instructions the prosecutor gave the SUP as to what action they should take?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That is what I wish to say. I have the prosecutor's Official Note here. In it he describes in detail what happened in Racak, and he gives his opinion and report on it. I don't think I have to read it. I have it in Serbian, and I don't know whether you have it among your own exhibits. Would you like me to read it out slowly in Serbian?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]... sorry. Sorry. The accused will be able to tell us if it is in the exhibits he's produced. If it's not, then it comes very late.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, is it among your exhibits?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't know what you're asking me, really, because I was looking at the papers that Mr. Nice just had distributed now.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Official Note of the public prosecutor dated the 9th of March, 1999. Is it an exhibit?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't know that just off-the-cuff. I haven't got all the binders here. I can't really say at this stage.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Perhaps I can read just one sentence from the Official Note and then the other evidence read out by -- submitted by the prosecutor. He described the event in Racak, and since he came to the conclusion that members of the police did not break the law on internal affairs, on the interior, and that they did not overstep their authority in relation to the action they took in Racak in order to find the perpetrators of the act of terrorism, after the post-mortem, when it was established that 37 bodies of victims had nitrate particles on their bodies, which demonstrates that they fired from firearms and that all the injuries sustained by the said persons were sustained from different directions and different weapons, which leads to the conclusion that the victims took action. Also that the firing was from a distance. And the last sentence is: "For the above-mentioned reasons, I believe that there are no grounds to take procedure with regard to any criminal offence according to which action has to be taken in line with official duty."
