Later on, the prosecutor submits a request to collect necessary information to the SUP in Urosevac, and that request has to do with the following: In relation to the mentioned crime, and the crime is --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Your Honour, could I ask for cite of that document and have it looked at?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes. I was going to ask the witness. What are you reading from?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have it right here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: What is it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's in my papers. I don't know whether it is in the Prosecution papers, but these are my personal documents. I myself have a set of documents in relation to Racak, and this is among the court records of Racak.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: What you just read out would have been an official instruction from the prosecutor to the SUP.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Your Honour, could I have cite of that? We could copy it and then I could review it, if necessary. But obviously if we're going to have documents produced like this, it's going to be difficult with the timetable.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes. Let the document be --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Mrs. Marinkovic, you said before the break that you weren't yourself expressing conclusions. That simply isn't true because you were brought here to express conclusions and you expressed several. I'm just going to tell you some of the conclusions that you gave. You said it is not correct that there had been shelling. It is not correct that on the hill, as it says here, 25 persons were brought out and killed. Now, what is that if it isn't a conclusion, Mrs. Marinkovic?

utterances.speaker: DANICA MARINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Those are facts, not conclusions. The facts that I observed directly.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Very well. If you had spoken, as others have, to a lieutenant colonel who's named to the 243rd VJ brigade, the liaison officer, who confirmed that the VJ had supported the MUP operation in Racak, you would not have been able to say there had been no shelling, would you?

utterances.speaker: DANICA MARINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know who this is. I don't know who this lieutenant colonel is. I am not aware of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... been referred to by a witness called Maisonneuve who did speak to him, and to Maisonneuve the lieutenant colonel made it quite plain that the VJ had supported the MUP operation in Racak with tank and Praga fire. If you had spoken to the same lieutenant colonel, you would not have been able to express as a conclusion that there had been no shelling, would you?

utterances.speaker: DANICA MARINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Give me a date. The name of the person that I talked to on that day as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: No, Mrs. Marinkovic. It's not for you to instruct me what to tell you. It's for you to answer questions, and my question to you is very clear: If or anybody in the investigation or judicial department had made inquiries of the army and had obtained information from Lieutenant Colonel Petkovic that he had -- Petrovic, I beg your pardon, that 243rd VJ Brigade had supported the MUP operation with tank and Praga fire, neither you nor your investigator would have been able to reach a conclusion that didn't allow for that; correct?

utterances.speaker: DANICA MARINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Nice, please don't be so upset and please don't raise your voice. I can hear you very well. I am telling you that I did not see any soldiers between the 15th and the 18th. I claim that with full responsibility that I did not see anyone from the army then. I'm not authorised to interview anyone from the army because the army is separate. They do not fall under the jurisdiction of the regular court.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And I won't accept correction from you either. I will speak to you as I judge appropriate. Let me make it quite clear, Mrs. Marinkovic: Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. You are being evasive and I'm going to suggest maybe worse, but I'll come to that later. If you are not able to interview people as important as the army, would you accept that you're not able to express any conclusion on this topic?

utterances.speaker: DANICA MARINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not talk to the military, and I did not reach any conclusions.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: What, therefore, was your observation to the Trial Chamber supposed to be if it wasn't a conclusion when you said, in terms, the people killed were not unarmed? What was that if it wasn't a conclusion?

utterances.speaker: DANICA MARINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I am just presenting facts that I observed and established directly.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: What was the following if it wasn't a conclusion, and I'll read another short answer of yours from 37784. "It shows that the village --" this was to do with the emptiness of the village -- "that the village had previously been liberated, that the civilians had left the village beforehand and that members of the terrorist gang or band had come in." What's that if it's not a conclusion from the evidence?

utterances.speaker: DANICA MARINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Again, these are facts that I observed directly on the spot.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Let's just look at a video, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Exhibit 95, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Have you ever taken the trouble to look at the exhibit in this case of what was seen in the gully? Have you?

utterances.speaker: DANICA MARINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If you referring to the video imagery that was on television when Walker entered Racak, I saw that, but only on television.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Well, it would have been open to you to have ask for and no doubt have been provided with a copy of the video produced years ago in this case to check whether there was anything on it that you wanted to bring to our attention. You've never done that. You see here the video taken of the people in the gully. I'm going to give you an opportunity through this and through some still photographs to add comments if you wish to.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: You say these men were not unarmed. You say that this was a battle. What do you want to tell us about this video? Anything you've seen so far? Because we can stop the video and you can tell us what's significant.

utterances.speaker: DANICA MARINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I saw this video clip on television, but the corpses, as far as I can see them now, on this footage in the mosque, among those 40, these were not the corpses that were there.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ...

utterances.speaker: DANICA MARINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I mean the clothing and the footwear in different colours, in bright colours, no. Well, you should ask Walker. Why did he not call me? Why didn't he wait for me to have a look at the bodies together? I cannot make comments now on his video footage. I can only make comments as to what I found in Racak and what I saw there.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And if the usher would be good enough, could we take perhaps the easel and the large plan or one of them. How many sites were there where dead bodies were found, Mrs. Marinkovic? How many?

utterances.speaker: DANICA MARINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've already said. The 40 corpses that we found in the mosque.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: How many sites were there where dead bodies were found? Do you know?

utterances.speaker: DANICA MARINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know about sites. I did not find any dead bodies at any sites that I toured or anything that would indicate that there had been bodies there.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Do you have any reason to challenge - and here's a map of Racak, it's an exhibit in a smaller form - and it shows 13 different locations for dead bodies being found, including the gully but including many others. Do you have any reason to doubt that dead bodies were found in all those different locations?

utterances.speaker: DANICA MARINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot orient myself on this map. This doesn't mean anything to me. I toured Racak itself. I was on the spot. As for the locations, I don't know what all these locations were and I don't know how many bodies you found and where exactly. This is the first time I hear of this, that there were several locations and that more bodies were found than the ones I found in the mosque.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: That's really your position, is it, that coming to this Court after all this time you haven't even acquainted yourself, as a judge, with the material that exists going to show where bodies were found and the condition in which they were seen and photographed before they were moved? Is that right?

utterances.speaker: DANICA MARINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't understand.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: You've made --

utterances.speaker: DANICA MARINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't understand the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: You have made no efforts and the accused has provided you with no material showing the condition of the bodies in which they were found?

utterances.speaker: DANICA MARINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Which bodies?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: The bodies at Racak.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Should we look at the photographs of Ian Hendrie, or some of them, please. They are Exhibit 156, tab -- starting at tab 5. Just a selection, bearing in mind what the witness said about belts in particular.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: A series of photographs. If you look at these photographs --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: That's the gully. Well, let's move on from that. Next one, please. Next one, please. Next one, please. Don't need those. Next. Keep going. I think it's the tagged ones. It's the tagged ones there, please, Mr. Prendergast.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: There you are. It's not very clear but have a look at that. Look at it on the overhead projector. Look at the type of belt the young man is wearing. That was photographed in position.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: If we go to the next tagged one, Mr. Prendergast, please, we'll find another belt, this time a blue belt. Next tagged one, please. There's a blue belt. We go to the next tagged one, please. I've tried to pick up all the photographs of people with belts, you see. See the belt there? Next photograph, please, Mr. Prendergast.

utterances.speaker: DANICA MARINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You know what? I have to ask you something. Where did these photographs come from? Who photographed the bodies? Who found the bodies? I don't understand any of this that you're showing me.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... on the 16th of January of 1999, by a man called Hendrie, and they were available for you to see in the course of your preparation to give evidence, no doubt, but you haven't been shown them. I'm sorry about that. It's not my fault. Look at the belt on the one that's on the picture at the moment, please.

utterances.speaker: DANICA MARINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Where is -- where are the victims? Where are these dead bodies?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Yes. You don't know the location so I haven't been troubling you with it, but if you want to know, I can tell you. Do you wish to know where this one was found?

utterances.speaker: DANICA MARINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: This is scene 5. If you look at location 5.

utterances.speaker: DANICA MARINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You know what? I cannot make any comments regarding bodies I did not find in Racak and that I did not see. The person who found them, who took all these photographs, why did he not come to me? Why did he not come to see me and to show me all of this on the 16th? I can just make comments on the bodies that I found on the 18th in the mosque in Racak. I cannot make any comments with regard to things that I have not seen myself.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Next tagged one, scene 3. You see, all the belts -- you said that the belts were similar or identical. You attached significance to it. The photographs taken at the time - it's a tiny point - show that they're all different. Why do you say there was significance, because that's what you did say, in the belts being the same? Why do you say that?

utterances.speaker: DANICA MARINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, you see, I have to draw your attention to something once again. I cannot make any comments regarding these bodies. I did not see them. I did not find them. No one informed me of their existence. I am making comments about the bodies that I found in the mosque on the 18th. In relation to this, I cannot give you any answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: It may be difficult to do, but are you not able to identify any of these bodies to see if they're the same as the witness saw?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: If we go to the end, and if the usher would go to, I think, the last three tags in the documents, he will find, I hope -- it's not in -- it may be in this section. Right at the end. The gully has actually been photographed, I'll make it available if Mr. Prendergast doesn't have it, to deal with His Honour's question. Mr. Prendergast, perhaps you'd like -- here they come. Go on these photographs towards the end, Mr. Prendergast, and it's right at the end of the collection. No. Just before that.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Now, you see here photographs have been made with the names of the victims written over them. So here we have Hapik Imeri, Ahmet Jakupi -- or Iseki, Esref Jakupi.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: The previous photograph, please, Mr. Prendergast. The previous one to that, I think. No. I think they're slightly out of order. Let me hand in mine if you can't find it. It's got the number 214999 at the top, right-hand corner.

utterances.speaker: DANICA MARINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know when this photograph was taken. It was winter. Here I can see green leaves and trees, so it's spring. I don't know when this one was taken here.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Very well. All taken at the same time. The bodies now, if you can see them, you see with all the names on them. The identifications have been drawn. All unarmed, some with belts, some with no belts, none with identical belts. These were the bodies that were found, Mrs. Marinkovic. And you've never considered the photographs.

utterances.speaker: DANICA MARINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The photographs or, rather, the person who compiled them could have brought me those in court and we could have looked at them together and dealt with them together. I can't comment on something that I haven't seen, didn't notice myself, didn't see. It's something new for me. So I did not take part in that. I did not see those bodies.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Well, of course --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: These two points you make, with respect, are inconsistent. You say the person who took the photographs could have bought them to you and you could have looked at them. Well, you've now got them, so you can now look at them. They can't be improved upon. They're there. So what Mr. Nice wants to know is whether you have a comment to make about the wearing of belts in the light of what you've now seen.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As far as the belts are concerned, that's just one detail. So among those 40 corpses we found in the mosque, among them -- I don't say all of them but among them-- there were those who were wearing the same or similar leather belts. That's what I can state. That indicates the fact that, taken in conjunction with the other evidence, a belt in itself is not essential, but if you compare the winter boots that they were wearing, or winter shoes and trousers and the weapons and the traces of gunpowder found on their hands, all this indicates that the participants were KLA members. And their headquarters was found, too. We found the remnants of their headquarters.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Now you're drawing conclusions, the thing you've told us repeatedly you're not permitted to do.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I am not drawing conclusions. All I am doing is taking note of the facts, the facts that I saw on the spot, noticed and recorded. They are facts, not conclusions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: To conclude, to conclude that any of these -- or to say that any of these people were KLA members requires you to draw a conclusion. It's so obvious, Mrs. Marinkovic, there's no point in disputing it, and you've done it repeatedly in your evidence.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Everything that I found on the spot, on site, indicates the fact that they were members of the KLA. That's it.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Can I show you three photographs that come from the same collection.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please. Microphone for Mr. Nice, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: They're from tab 7 of Mr. Hendrie's exhibits. If you'd followed the evidence in this case, Mrs. Marinkovic, you'd know that this young boy was injured, went to hospital, and came back to point out where events had happened.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Next photograph, please, Mr. Prendergast. Next one.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: There he is again. First of all, there's no suggestion, is there, in the conflict in Kosovo that boys of this youth - I know it happens in other parts of the world sometimes, tragically - but there's no suggestion, is there, that boys of this youth were involved in violence, is there?

utterances.speaker: DANICA MARINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: And who is the boy? When was this photograph taken? Is the boy one of the 40 corpses that I have on my list?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Please listen to the question. I told you he was in hospital. He was wounded. He came back to point out where things had happened. My question to you was quite clear: Is there any suggestion that people of this youth were involved in violence on the part of the KLA?

utterances.speaker: DANICA MARINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have a piece of information here according to which one boy was a casualty, but let me tell you the children -- children didn't take part, but they helped. They brought in food, water --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I see.

utterances.speaker: DANICA MARINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- carried information.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: But if he was a survivor, because he was only injured, and if he was in hospital, you could have talked to him or your prosecutor could have talked to him. Can you explain to the judges why -- don't just go to the system of your courts, we know about that. Can you just explain why it is that no one took the opportunity of speaking to an eyewitness like this?

utterances.speaker: DANICA MARINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: And why didn't the boy ask to be interviewed or why didn't the parents come in to report it? I don't know where the boy was from, but in Stimlje and in Racak --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... answer and I'm going to move on. I'll give you another chance to think about that answer: Why did no one take the opportunity of speaking to an eyewitness in hospital, like this?

utterances.speaker: DANICA MARINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Nobody knew that the boy was an eyewitness.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Now, let me ask you one more question before we move to your central evidence, as it may be, on membership of the KLA. I asked you before the break if this was a conflict between the KLA and the police, I want to know why the police account isn't available to us. Let me go back to your earlier years as a more junior judge. Did you ever deal in allegations of Mr. A hitting Mr. B, something as simple as that? Did you?

utterances.speaker: DANICA MARINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I had cases like that too.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Very well. Thank you. In such cases, it would be necessary, wouldn't it, and obvious, to obtain both sides' evidence, if possible?

utterances.speaker: DANICA MARINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When there is a concrete individual who is the perpetrator of a crime, and if there is a specific and if we know who the party afflicted is, so we first interview the accused and then we interview the injured party. That's how an investigation is conducted. And then we amass other evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: DANICA MARINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: And pursuant to the prosecutor's request --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... your inference, your guess, your hope was that this was a battle between the KLA as wrongdoers and the police was rightdoers, why has no one taken the account of the police? It's so obvious, Mrs. Marinkovic. What wasn't it done?

utterances.speaker: DANICA MARINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At that stage as conducted by me, the investigation, I wasn't authorised except to carry out an on-site scene of crime investigation to enter into any other proceedings without an order from the prosecutor.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Can you help us with why the prosecutor, if this is the case - we haven't seen all the papers - didn't get an account from what would be the victim of the unlawful attack by the KLA? Can you help us, please?

utterances.speaker: DANICA MARINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't understand your question. How do you mean "victim"?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Very well. If you didn't understand the question, I won't press any further, and I'll ask you --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mrs. Marinkovic, could you remind me of one thing: How many casualties were there on the police side?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If you just mean Racak and the surrounding parts, then I don't know the exact number, but certainly dozens of policemen were killed in the area during that time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: No, I mean on the day of the incident. On the 15th of January, 1999, how many casualties were there on the police side in this confrontation that resulted, as you suggest, in the death of the large number of Kosovo Albanians?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think was it one policeman who was killed and three injured, or the other way around, I don't know. But there is a report by SUP and a criminal report that was filed, and the wounded or injured policemen were interviewed with respect to the incident, and the papers exist in the SUP of Urosevac. I know for sure they have the files on that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Do we have a narrative account somewhere from the police of what they did, where they went, when they went there, how it was that their members died? Do we have that anywhere?

utterances.speaker: DANICA MARINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that an official report about that exists, both with respect to the Urosevac SUP and with respect to the MUP of Serbia.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: But it's not here with you. It's not something upon which you rely for your opinion.

utterances.speaker: DANICA MARINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not authorised for that, nor could I delve into it.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Your Honours, just give me one minute.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: My suggestion to you, Mrs. Marinkovic, following on indeed from His Honour's query, is that if this had been in any sense a fight, there would have been more than just injuries effectively all on one side, or with a large number killed on one side, and I must suggest to you that when you went there, you went there on the instructions of the police to provide some kind of cover for the enormous number of dead bodies that would have to be processed in some way. Isn't that the truth?

utterances.speaker: DANICA MARINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is why I insisted and wanted to conduct an on-site investigation, to determine and establish the facts and not to cover them up. And what I did find on site I took note of and recorded, and there is Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. written trace of it all; my official notes and my official reports.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Can we go, please, to your tab 52, which is in English and Serbian. This was not a statement taken by you yourself, was it?

utterances.speaker: DANICA MARINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: It was simply taken by -- who is Dragan Jasovic and Momcilo Sparavalo?

utterances.speaker: DANICA MARINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I haven't got the second page.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Who are these people who took the statement?

utterances.speaker: DANICA MARINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They are officials working in the Urosevac SUP.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Does that mean police or does it mean something else?

utterances.speaker: DANICA MARINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. They were civilian people working in the Urosevac SUP. They weren't policemen, didn't wear uniforms. They were crime inspectors, if that explains it better.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Your Honours, may we go into private session for just less than a minute.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, private session.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Looking at tab 52, the statement taken by Jasovic and Sparavalo, there is no way that you can help us, is there, with the accuracy or otherwise of that statement? You can't express any opinion about it, can you?

utterances.speaker: DANICA MARINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This statement was taken by officials from the citizens that gave them, and I can just say that this statement was taken with compliance to the law and is a component part of the documentation I had for Racak and sent on to the prosecutor.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: You weren't present when the 16-year-old boy was interviewed, were you?

utterances.speaker: DANICA MARINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: You would accept as a judge and investigator that an appropriate way of checking whether the statement is accurate is to go and ask the boy, or now the young man.

utterances.speaker: DANICA MARINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, it's not up to me. It doesn't come within my authority to investigate and check out.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... if we need to check the accuracy of the statement, the appropriate course to do is to go and ask him, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: DANICA MARINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the individuals said what they wanted to say in the statement, what they had to say.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... check the accuracy of three or four statements that associate victims with membership of the KLA, you as an investigative judge would accept that the appropriate course, as a judge or prosecutor or whatever, you would accept that the appropriate course is to speak to all three of them, because only three are now alive, and to deal with them separately in circumstances where they can't speak to each other between interviews. Would you accept that that's an appropriate and careful way to proceed?

utterances.speaker: DANICA MARINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The statement taken by officials from citizens, there's nothing to doubt, and there's no need to check it, because they were officials who take these statements from citizens in the manner prescribed by law. So there's no need for any subsequent checks to be made. Only if there is doubt, and in this case there was no doubt because a large number of citizens presented the same facts which coincide when you put the pieces of the mosaic together to form a whole.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Mrs. Marinkovic, we looked at, at an earlier stage in your judicial career, one complaint in detail in relation to the police case. There are several hours that I could have put to you in relation to that, and I must suggest to you that with the complaints of which you were aware about people being beaten, your last answer is simply unrealistic. There's always the chance that people are going to be persuaded to say things that are untrue. Do you not accept that?

utterances.speaker: DANICA MARINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do not accept that, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Every statement taken --

utterances.speaker: DANICA MARINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In this specific case -- would you just listen, hear me out. When an individual comes to me pursuant to a request from the prosecutor for me to conduct an investigation, that individual tells me what he considers is his defence. If he does not know Serbian, then he avails himself of the use of a interpreter, and the defence counsel is present too. So what that person considers he needs to tell me and before me as the investigating judge, he does so and I record it. Now, all the things that you mention, I didn't use any of that, and I say that with full responsibility. Now, you can check out wherever you like an accused that I interviewed. Nobody ever complained about my work. None of the parties involved. I continued to work normally in court. I continued to move around Pristina normally, to socialise with people, with colleagues, et cetera, so that these assertions of yours are completely unfounded. That's all I wish to say.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Your Honours, the witnesses available, one being dead, have been seen. In each case, interviews with them were videoed for two reasons. In addition to a video, a short written statement was taken. My intention, because a video would take too long to play, is to play a small clip from each of the three videos and then to present to the witness in the court the statements that summarise the position of the witness. With your leave, I will now play a short clip from the interview conducted since the court last sat of Afrim Mustafa.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Nice, let us -- we're going to consider that.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Certainly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, you may have the video played.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. [Videotape played]: "Is it you say a room like that? And what happened in that room? "And they were saying that -- that I've been member of KLA, and then they asked me to touch the wires. "They asked you to touch some wires? Were the wires connected to anything? "I couldn't see anything like in the floor, because it was covered, but I could see a box where they put the switch, the button. "And just to be clear, I want to understand -- just to be clear on the language, were you asked to touch some wires or were you told to touch some wires? "I was urged to touch the wires. "All right. And did you touch the wires? "At first they -- they touched the wires themselves, but the button wasn't switched on. "Uh-huh. "So they told me, 'You see? Nothing will happen if you touch.' And initially when I touched the wires, nothing happened. "Uh-huh. "And then when I touched them again, they switched on the button. "Uh-huh. "I felt a shock and I started to cry and scream. "Uh-huh. "They started to shout at me. "What were they shouting? "'You have been a member of the army of KLA.'"

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I would like to distribute a statement. Your Honours, of course the whole tape is available to the accused and the amicus, whatever its evidential status may be decided to be --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: What was the name of this witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Afrim Mustafa.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Tab 52.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: The same one, sorry, Your Honour, yes. And then the content of the interview, in order to be economic with time, the content was summarised in a short statement, and signed, and I'm going to go through a couple of the paragraphs with this witness and ask for her comments.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Mrs. Marinkovic, this young man, who was 16, explained that on the 16th of January - this is the second paragraph - he went to Stimlje and stopped by the police, hit on the legs and put in a police car, he being with an old man, asked for their names and where they were from, accused of being members of the KLA. The police said, "How can you be alive? We killed all the people there." He goes on to say the police took him to the police station in Ferizaj, cursing mothers, as it were, and taking them for interrogation where he was interrogated by three men in a room who accused him of being a member of the KLA. He then goes on to deal with the box, the switch, the wires and the second time of touching of the wires when he screamed. He explains that they also hit him on his hands with sticks. He didn't give the men any information because he was unable to. One of the men was writing something on a computer, and eventually one of the men said, "Let him go, he's only a child." Before we look to see what he says about membership of the KLA and about the statement, can you comment, please, on how this person, who apparently gave this voluntary statement, gives an account like this? Is it because perhaps it's true and that's the way your police officers or investigators behaved?

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: She can't, and that's the whole point of this. I've been allowing it to develop because I didn't want anyone -- to be thought that we unnecessarily take objections or we're being obstructive, but it's useful sometimes to see how this material develops. There's no connection between the young man in the statement and this witness in any way. There's no crossover between her evidence and his evidence on a direct basis, and in those circumstances she can't possibly comment on what was in his mind, why he acted in a particular way, and what his acts and conduct were. And having allowed this to develop so that the Court can see really the basis of our standing objection in relation to this line of cross-examination, this is a classic example that illustrates the point that we have made on a number of previous occasions as well as in our filings.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Kay. The Chamber agrees with you. Mr. Nice, you may be able to put another question that the witness can answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Yes. Can I therefore take the witness to the next passage of the interview -- of the record and come back to a question that I may wish to ask.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: You see, the statement goes on, Mrs. Marinkovic, to say that this young man was shown this tab 52 of your exhibits, and he explained that he didn't sign the statement and that the signature is not his. As to membership of the KLA or not, he sets out a number of people - and if we look at them, Your Honours, it's 1, 3, 4, 5, 6, 7, and 8 - who he says were not members of the KLA. Afet Bilalli, who is not listed in the indictment who he says was a member of the KLA, and number 5, Muhamet Mustafa, son of Hafiz, who he says he's not sure about. Now, this statement, you see, Mrs. Marinkovic, comes from, it would appear, the same young man as identified in tab 52 and gives an account that I've just summarised for you. I come back to my first question. There is no way in the circumstances, rather as Mr. Kay implied when he was asking -- raising an objection, there's no way you can say what was in the mind of the young man --

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: We're on the same territory, and --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Nice, I don't see the point in pursuing this line.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, my position to the witness is that this witness -- he's not a witness; this young man was forced into signing this statement -- not forced into signing the statement, didn't sign the statement, and the document that you have produced is not his in any sense.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Again, I find it difficult to see how she can answer that. And you have a brilliant way of establishing this, Mr. Nice, which will be to do some handwriting comparisons.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: In due course.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Indeed. But we've taken again a little time on this. I know I'm demonstrating impatience this morning, but I do genuinely feel it, that there has been a period of time in the course of the cross-examination today which has been extremely productive, but there has been, I regret to say, a lot that doesn't strike me as productive. And this is an example, because what's happened here is you've presented material which you can't present at this stage when a simple question could have been asked of the witness without going through a video and then presenting a statement, which I think you must have known she wasn't really able to make -- wouldn't be able to make a serious comment about. Now, that may show certain deficiencies in her processes, for all I know, and that can be addressed in due course, but it's not a matter that's going to be expanded upon usefully in cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: As Your Honour pleases, but my problem remains that I have to put our case. Until the witness gives evidence, we don't know what her evidence is going to be, and I can only put my case --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: But you're not obliged to put a case that she can't comment on. You're only obliged to put your case to people who can sensibly comment about the case you're actually putting.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: With very great respect, Your Honour, Your Honour's observation shows the severe limitations and difficulties with this witness being allowed to produce material of this potential significance in this form when the witnesses themselves would have been available to be called. Because if it's said that she's able to say, as she did, this is a reliable statement because it's taken in conformity with practices of the court, and it's what she does say both by implication and expressly, but I'm not able to say to her, but look -- and we did this, of course, with the most recent witness, his name I've temporarily forgotten, who produced a statement, if I'm not able to put to the witness the contrary statement or the contrary video, then the issues are not really joined and the Chamber isn't really being assisted. And, Your Honour, I would wish to deal with the other two witnesses in broadly the similar way, showing the statements that have been taken from them, showing the short clips of video in each case of their interviews and drawing to your attention their expressions of opinion as to membership of the KLA, because -- that's what I would wish to do.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Let me try something with the witness just now. Mrs. Marinkovic, if you discovered that a witness who gave a statement that you were considering in the course of an investigation had been tortured, would you give any weight at all to that statement? Simple question.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. If a person had complained to me and said something like that, I certainly would have taken action.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Just listen to the question. If you learned that a witness who had given a statement had been tortured in the course of giving that statement, would you give that statement any weight at all in your investigation?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You see, if that is proven that the statement was given under such circumstances, it would certainly be taken into account that that statement could not constitute evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. My second question: If you learned that the witness's signature had been forged on the statement, would you take it into account? Would you take the statement into account in any way?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Again, if the signature is proven to be forged, it cannot be reliable evidence. If that is proven, of course?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: With Your Honours' leave, I would deal with the same Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. short exercise, and I can deal with it shortly with the other two witnesses who are still alive so that the Trial Chamber can know what material exists. The next one would be --

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: No. I think we need a review of all this because otherwise we're going down the same route. It's the introduction of material in this way that eventually gets discounted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I thought Mr. Nice was departing from that, but I have maybe misunderstood.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I'm hoping to do the same exercise with the other two.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And Your Honours will have in mind that Lituchy, in Lituchy's case the contrary statement was put in. The history of this exercise has been we were presented at short witness with hearsay material of potential significance. We inquire into it. We present our findings fully. In relation to the first witness - it was Andric, was it not? - a video was played of a contrary interpretation of events by the person interviewed, the video was not produced as an exhibit, but I think we were told then that we were allowed to put this for the comment of the witness. With Lituchy, similar things happened, but in light of the Chamber's position on the video, we produced a statement, a contrary statement, as it were, a statement putting the contrary position of the person interviewed was admitted. On this occasion, arguably the evidence much more significant than the earlier evidence because this goes to a central issue about Racak, we obviously have to investigate, and I said when I sought the Chamber's leave to rise 15 minutes early, so I wasn't going to -- wish to be putting assertions to the witness without having done the investigations because it wouldn't have been a responsible course. We've done the investigation. Because of the earlier practices, we've done both things: We've got a video recording and a short statement that sets out the position of the witness. Now, I can either say, if I'm confined to this extent, I must suggest to you, Mrs. Marinkovic, that the statement isn't true, and the Chamber isn't assisted at all, or I can lay out in a couple of minutes what our position is and leave it for the Chamber to decide following discussion what evidential status that material can fill. And it would be my submission that, at the very least, the position with Lituchy should be followed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, you may put -- put it, Mr. Nice.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Well, I'm very much obliged. May I take it that I can put a short passage from --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: It's time to adjourn for the 20-minute break.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I'll deal with it very quickly, if I can, afterwards, and in each case I'll put a short clip - I've prepared them - of the video interviews, and a summary of the statements. I can even make the statements available in advance, if you'd like to see them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes. We'll adjourn for 20 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Nice.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: We'll play a short extract from a video recorded interview with somebody called Muhadin Dzeljadini at tab 51 of the Defence exhibits. [Videotape played]: "Let's go back a little bit to the 17th of January when you were in Ferizaj. So at some point on that day, on the 17th of January, you were asked to sign a statement; is that correct? "That's correct. "All right. And that -- "I didn't want to sign it but I was urged to sign it. Because when I saw the blood on the -- at the basement, I was so afraid. So I -- I signed it. "Okay. So -- so -- in other words, are you telling --"

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Where did this interview by Investigator Saxon take place?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: The interview was conducted in Pristina.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Pristina.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Yes, the field office. And the holiday was sacrificed in order that the interview be made.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Oh.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And if we could look, please, at the statement briefly.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: You see, this statement taken over the last few days by an investigator and a lawyer, explains in the second paragraph how this man had indeed been told to leave the village by William Walker because he said the Serbs are coming. How on the 17th of January he went to Stimlje, detained by the police who said that he'd been up in the mountains. He denies being a member of the KLA. He was taken to room number 51 in the police station. He told the men that on the previous day, the 16th, he had been in Racak and had helped move the bodies to the mosque, and indeed included in the bodies he'd dealt with was the decapitated body that we know about and have seen in photographs. He was then beaten with a stick, asked why he was saying such things, was taken to a smaller room and asked about provisioning for the KLA, saying he didn't know, sent to the basement which had a room about six metres long, four men present who pressed him to accept what they said, in particular wanting him to say that a man called Mehmet Mustafa had a rocket launcher, whereas the person knew it only to be a gun, acknowledging that Mehmet Mustafa was indeed a member of the KLA. Pressed to make concessions about Sadik Mujota, his visit to the station ended when he was asked to sign a statement, which is our tab 51. He acknowledges that the signature is his, but he didn't want to sign it and he said that there was blood on the floor of the basement, that he was afraid. I'll come back to that in a second. Paragraph 7 he says Mehmet Mustafa was a member of the KLA. He didn't know about Lutfi Bilalli, and as to Nijazi Zymberi, he was not a member of the KLA but he doesn't know about Bajram Mehmeti. Did you go to the basement where these people were interrogated, Mrs. Marinkovic?

utterances.speaker: DANICA MARINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have no comment regarding this question, nor do I have an answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Following on from the question that His Honour Judge Bonomy asked you before the break, if you knew that a signature had been appended by someone to a statement, having been beaten, would you pay any attention to the contents of that statement?

utterances.speaker: DANICA MARINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've already given an answer to Judge Bonomy. If I understood you correctly, because I do not have a Serbian translation of this witness's statement, the citizen you interviewed after so many years did not deny it. He said that he did sign this signature, that it is his signature. It is for the Trial Chamber to decide now the statement that he gave in 1999 and the statement that you took from him now a few days ago which one is more reliable. That will be for the Trial Chamber to decide. I would like to say another thing. The witnesses you interviewed now, they are afraid for safety and security reasons to confirm what they said in 1999, so they are telling you what they said to you. The degree of truthfulness of this is a different matter.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Mrs. Marinkovic, do you remember a short exchange between yourself and Judge Bonomy where he asked you questions about whether you were drawing conclusions? Is what you've just told us a conclusion?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Nice, that was in relation to a different matter, an entirely different matter.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I want to know is what the witness telling us now -- is what she's telling us now about the witnesses being afraid a conclusion, Mrs. Marinkovic?

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Well, if you're putting material like this, you're going to invite responses like that, and in a way, the Prosecution have brought this on themselves.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: I don't see the point of the question, Mr. Nice.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I'd like to press it with this: Mrs. Marinkovic, you're in no position to say, seeing two different statements and somebody saying it was taken -- no, I won't bother. I won't press it. It will only be argumentative. Can we look at the third clip, please, which is tab 47.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I take it that you are content that the answer you got to the question you asked was, depends on circumstances, that that sort of statement might well be given some weight. At least, that's what I draw from the answer, that the judge wouldn't reject that sort of statement out of hand.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm quite, in a sense, happy with that as a conclusion because if the Chamber is going to be invited in due course to act at all on the conclusions, although she denies making them, of this witness, and the Chamber knows that she's somebody who would not rule out of hand statements obtained by force, then the Chamber may be confronting a different approach to the general standards of admissibility from those that it would apply itself. So I'm happy enough with her answer. It would be my submission, and indeed I can remember His Honour Judge Robinson dealing with this at an early stage and expressing an opinion on the matter, in my submission, that modern standards would make any statement obtained following coercion of no value to a Chamber. His Honour Judge Robinson dealt with that specifically.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, it's surprising that wasn't the answer you were given.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Your Honour, yes indeed.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Can we just then look briefly at the third one which is, yes, tab 47, Shemsi Emini. [Videotape played]: "There were two police on that side carrying baseball bats. "Uh-huh. "... baseball bats. And they started to beat me everywhere apart from the face. "Uh-huh. And how long were you beaten? "So they were beating me like for ten minutes, an hour, and they interrogated me again. "All right. So as they were beating you and interrogating you, what kinds of things were they asking you? "They asked me about some people of Racak village, whether do I know these people. They were saying names. "Uh-huh."

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. If we can look at the statement taken from the same person. A little longer but I'll deal with it shortly.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: If we look at the second page, Mrs. Marinkovic, even if you don't speak English or don't speak it fluently, and I'm not sure of your level of English, you will see that in paragraph 6 he makes it clear that he's shown the statement, tab 47, which is the tab that you produced of this person, and you'll see that he acknowledges the signature as being his, and he says he didn't sign it voluntarily but was forced to do so. And then if we come back to pages 1 -- or page 1, he wanted to go to the funeral of those who died in Racak, was stopped by a policeman who alleged he was a terrorist. Paragraph 3, was interrogated on his own, explained his reason for wanting to go to Racak, was asked by policemen who killed somebody, his cousin Ajak Emini [phoen] or Brahimi, and he said that the Serb police killed him. The policemen replied that they didn't, that the KLA did, and he said that the KLA would not kill its own people. And then they used their baseball bats or similar to beat him. And they also asked about different people, at one stage mentioning Ragip Bajrami and asked if he was a member of the KLA, the man Shemsi Emini saying, "No, he's a civilian, like me," knowing that he, Ragip Bajrami was killed in Racak but not daring to mention his name. Now, do you have any comments to make about -- they then threatened him with prison and asked him about money, and he explained that he'd given money to a civilian in Racak. Do you have any comment to make on this man who says that he was compelled to sign this statement?

utterances.speaker: DANICA MARINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Any comment would be superfluous. After so many years, what is true? But read every record, every statement that witnesses, citizens gave with the authorised officials. It says very nicely down here that he read the statement, recognised it as his own, and confirms that with his signature. And now you found him five years later and you're saying that he gave the statement under duress. What kind of proof do you have that the statement that you obtained now is correct and authentic? Just like you are doubting the one he gave to me, I am doubting the one he gave you, especially in view of the fact that he gave me the statement in 1999, immediately after the said events, and you heard him so many years later.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Gave you or gave your offices?

utterances.speaker: DANICA MARINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no, no. To the authorised officials, in the legally prescribed form.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Your Honours, I'm --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] With all his details. He gave all his details and he gave a proper account. How could the officials know all these details if he did not provide them himself? He described in detail everything he knew.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Mrs. --

utterances.speaker: DANICA MARINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: And here in the statement that you obtained, they're only interested in saying what you are interested in hearing from them, that is whether they gave those statements under duress or when they were tortured.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Your Honours, it will take a few minutes but I think it must be worthwhile. The document that the witness produced which hadn't been produced by the accused would appear to be the only extant, or at least the only presently existing, account by the local police of what happened. It's not in translation. It's about a half a page long, and with Your Honours' leave, may it go on the overhead projector, a copy go in front of the witness, and may we have it read in full rather than the selective statements that she chose.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Which is Official Note by the prosecutor.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: That's correct, yes. And then I have about two questions to ask her of it. But it seems to me better to get the document in while she's here in case it stimulates any questions by the Court and indeed in re-examination but since she's produced some sentences from it. If she could have it in front of her so she could read it and the interpreters could translate it.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Mrs. Marinkovic, I'm going to ask you to read all of the paragraph -- perhaps we'll start from about six lines up on the first paragraph, "MUP RS Koja su," and then we go from there, 15/1/99. If you could read it, but please will you remember that the interpreters have to interpret and there is a temptation to read documents too rapidly. If you could just start and read out loud starting with "Koja su 15.1.1999."

utterances.speaker: DANICA MARINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: So you mean to start from here.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Yes, please.

utterances.speaker: DANICA MARINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: "The RS MUP who on the 15th of January, 1999, undertook action to apprehend the perpetrators of the crime of terrorism which crime was committed against the now late Svetislav Przic and the abduction of a number of citizens of Albanian nationality or ethnicity loyal to the state of Serbia and the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia and that all the actions undertaken were geared towards refuting an armed attack by members of the terrorist band, the so-called KLA, and in conformity with the law on internal affairs." Do you want me to read on?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: DANICA MARINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: "From the Official Note of the investigating judge of the district court in Pristina, the crime number was 14/99 and the date the 15th of January, 1999, the Official Notes of the deputy district public prosecutor and the chronological list of events by the SUP of Urosevac, along with photographic documentation number 15/99 of the 15th of January, 1999, and number 23/99 of the 18th of January, 1999, undoubtedly establish that on the 15th of January, 1999, in the early morning hours, in the area of the village of Racak, there was a mass -- there were mass armed attacks against members of the police force by members of the terrorist band, the so-called KLA, from a number of directions with weapons of different calibre and great destructive power and from a number of fortified positions as well as from apartment buildings in the settlement itself. On that occasion, a policeman Goran Vicentijevic received bodily injuries and a criminal report was filed because of that against perpetrators unknown, KU number 9/99, dated the 29th of January, 1999, and it was recorded in the prosecutor's office under the number of KTN 43/99. In refuting the attack, 40 members of the so-called KLA were killed who had taken part directly in the attack or undertaken action for its successful completion. This conclusion, without a doubt, emanates from a finding by the crime technicians of the SUP of Pristina, number 03234/1/66-99 of the 21st of January, 1999, from which it emerges that with 37 corpses, the presence of nitrate particles and nitrite particles were found which may have come from gunpowder (except for on the corpses numbered 11, 24, and 28) and from the conclusions of the Institute for Forensic Medicine of the medical faculty in Pristina, UV number 75/99, that all the injuries on the corpses were inflicted during their lifetime (intra-vital ones) and they were sustained through firearms on different portions and parts of the body from different directions which indicates us to conclude that it was that the victims were in the -- engaged in some action and that they were inflicted from a distance except in the case of two bodies, bodies 24 and 34, where we have excluded immediate proximity, but in view of the number of injuries on these bodies, we cannot exclude a relative distance at the moment the injury was inflicted. "For the reasons presented above, I consider that there is no grounds for taking proceedings further in -- for any crime where Prosecution is indicated pursuant to authority and competence."

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Two or three questions, Mrs. Marinkovic, and I'll be done with this document. When you spoke earlier of a death, the death was a death that had happened before the attack at Racak. It was the death of Svetislav Przic; is that right?

utterances.speaker: DANICA MARINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. The cause for the operation in Racak.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Because that was the immediate genesis of Racak. The KLA had, it appears, killed a policeman, and the police went in to attack Racak. And that's what this document reveals, although it tries in a way to obscure it. Is that the truth? A revenge attack for the death of a policeman?

utterances.speaker: DANICA MARINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. No, that's not correct. The police went to find the perpetrators of the act and crime of terrorism. That was the pretext for the attack. That was why the attack came, and that's what it says in the Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. note.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Now let's look at something else that's -- you see -- let's look at something else that this statement or summary reveals, and perhaps you would be good enough to have in mind the map beside you and so that the Judges can be reminded, the figure 5 shows the gully where the 20-odd men were found. But if you look around at all the other scenes marked 1 to 13, including over there on Cesta hill, that's where all the other people who died made up the 40 altogether. You understand, Mrs. Marinkovic, that photographs were taken of those bodies in situ on all those different 13 sites, and it's only by adding up all those different sites that you reach the figure of about 40. So do we take it that this -- would you understand this statement, assuming that the learned Judges here find that the bodies were found in the places where they were found, do you take it that this is an acknowledgement by the local police that they killed all those 40 people in all those different locations?

utterances.speaker: DANICA MARINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know where the bodies were found. I came across them in the mosque, and there were 40 of them in all.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Yes. You're the person with experience of the judicial system. This is a report from which you read a few sentences. I've now read all of it. Do you take it, assuming that 40 bodies were found in the 13 different locations - it's your system - may we take it that this is an acknowledgement by the police through this reporting mechanism that they killed all those 40 people? Can you look at the photographs, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Nice, why don't you just ask the question without the hypothesis. In other words, does the report amount to an acknowledgement that the police killed the 40 people, and then it's really for us to work out the rest, is it not?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: But it's more likely to produce an answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Does it amount to an acknowledgement, His Honour's question, that the police killed 40 people? Does it?

utterances.speaker: DANICA MARINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The police do not acknowledge having killed 40 people, in this Official Note what it says is that it took part in an operation to uncover the perpetrators of a crime and that it was during that operation that there was crossfire and that there was a conflict between the two sides, two parties. There was a lot of shooting. One side shot and the other side shot and it was in that conflict that these people fell victim, the ones that we found. Now, whether the policemen killed them or not, I'm not authorised to comment. But it is undoubtable that --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Mrs. Marinkovic, two points emerge. You're speaking of crossfire and earlier when you read selectively from this paragraph you led us to believe that a policeman had been killed. We now see that one policeman is actually recorded as injured. Can you just read again, please, that sentence that begins [B/C/S spoken] and then a reference to 40. Just read it for us once more, please.

utterances.speaker: DANICA MARINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's only for me to read it. You know what happens during a conflict, a conflict between two sides. What do you want me to read, which sentence?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: The sentence that has the figure 40 in it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Point her to the place where that is, Mr. Nice.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Yes. It's halfway down the second paragraph. The sentence begins [B/C/S spoken].

utterances.speaker: DANICA MARINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. "Repelling the attack, 40 members of the so-called KLA were killed, deprived of life, who had taken direct part in the attack or done actions to ensure its successful completion. This conclusion, without a doubt -- this conclusion, undoubtedly --"

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Last point on this document: There's reference to the nitrate test. You know as an experienced judge, prosecutor, what you will, that the nitrate test on its own is not sufficient for proving possession of firearms?

utterances.speaker: DANICA MARINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This test, it is true, does not in itself constitute evidence. However, the test itself is an indication that -- to the effect that a person had fired from a firearm. The gunpowder particles, once they were found and when they were found on the hand between the index finger and the second finger on the upper portion of the hand, indicates that the person did indeed hold a firearm and fire from the firearm. The presence of gunpowder particles. And as an investigative judge, I applied the test in numerous cases, taken, of course, together with all the other evidence which leads to an incontestable fact.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: If you're saying in respect of any of these dead men or the young woman that you found gunpowder particles between their fingers, you must point us to where it's recorded, because I may have missed it.

utterances.speaker: DANICA MARINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The prosecutor refers here to the findings. I am not an expert in the field myself, but I engaged a forensic ballistics expert, and issued orders for him to do the paraffin glove test to establish the presence or otherwise of gunpowder particles. And we have the finding. The prosecutor in his report refers to the finding by the crime technician of the SUP of Pristina, and the number is 234/1/66 or, rather, -1-66/99. The date is the 21st of January, 1999, from which it emerges that in 37 of the bodies the presence of nitrate particles was established. Nitrate particles were found to be present on 37 bodies.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... nitrate test.

utterances.speaker: DANICA MARINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, but which can -- can have been derived from gunpowder is the continuation of that sentence.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: We move on from Racak, very briefly, to deal with a couple of other things. So far as Dubrava Prison is concerned, you interviewed no survivors other than those you say you saw who had been injured and moved to the location where you were, the town where you were. You interviewed no other survivors, did you?

utterances.speaker: DANICA MARINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, yes, right.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: You --

utterances.speaker: DANICA MARINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Just let me say, and you didn't wait for me to complete my answer, since a large number of people who were wounded and injured from Dubrava were transferred to Lipljan, I did have the opportunity of seeing those people. However, I wasn't able to talk to them directly because they were under stress and they had been injured. So the essential thing to do first was to provide them with the medical care and attention they needed. Later on, we did talk to those people but not -- I didn't. We agreed with the prison authorities to talk to the people in question so that they could tell them what had happened while they were in Dubrava in the prison there.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: You produced your colleagues' report which we've looked at on the last occasion we were here, a couple of weeks ago, and he didn't speak to any of the survivors who have given evidence in this court, either Musan Krasniqi, Milaim Ceki or Gani Bekaj, did he?

utterances.speaker: DANICA MARINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know who these people are. I haven't heard of the names before.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Another example of the way in your country, or at least at the time of your holding office in the period with which we are concerned, another indication of the way inquiries were conducted, Mrs. Marinkovic, is the Kelmendi inquiry. Mr. and Mrs. Kelmendi were human rights lawyers, were they not, and they appeared often in your cases in defence of people charged with offences.

utterances.speaker: DANICA MARINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. And cooperation was perfectly proper at the official level, defence counsel/judge, that relationship. Perfectly proper.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... perhaps the most famous lawyer of his kind, was taken from his family with his two sons immediately after the bombing started and was eventually shot with his two sons, and you were the investigative judge, weren't you? Well, you've got a document out --

utterances.speaker: DANICA MARINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Just a moment, please. Bajram Kelmendi was an exceptional lawyer and a good criminal lawyer, and during the NATO bombing he wasn't shot as you say. Linked to that event, I as the investigating judge carried an on-site -- carried out an on-site investigation because the duty officer told me or informed me that three bodies had been found in that particular location. They didn't know who the bodies belonged to, and I went on site to establish the facts. And I'll show you the minutes, the record. I have all my records and minutes with me. I can tell you the exact day --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... me this: Did you ever go to Mrs. Kelmendi --

utterances.speaker: DANICA MARINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Just let me tell you, let me finish. Let me just tell you this --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... because it's the question I wanted to ask. Did you go to Mrs. Kelmendi and ever take from her an account of how her husband and sons had been taken from them and by whom they'd been taken?

utterances.speaker: DANICA MARINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: She came to see me in my office in the courtroom -- in court several times, and I talked to her, and she told me that that evening some unknown men turned up and took her husband off and her sons off, and when she -- when she came to see me, she said that we still didn't know where they were, whether they were dead or alive. So during the days that she came to see me in my office in the courthouse, we didn't know about their fate at all. It was only on the 26th of March, 1999, when I went on the spot to investigate and when three bodies were found by the roadside, and her brother was also present on that occasion when the on-site investigation took place, and I record this in my minutes and notes, he recognised them and said that the bodies were those of Bajram, Kastriot and Kushtrim Kelmendi. I compiled a report on my on-site investigation and sent it on to the Forensic Medical Institute for post-mortem to be conducted. I have it under the crime number. I have the number here of the case in question --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ...

utterances.speaker: DANICA MARINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- Kri number.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... taken her husband and her two sons. Has anybody ever been arrested for that crime?

utterances.speaker: DANICA MARINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You know what? Since the perpetrators were unknown, a criminal report was tabled by the SUP in Pristina and sent to the prosecutor in Pristina. On the 3rd of May 1999 there is a criminal report against perpetrators unknown for the crime of murder under Article 47, killing, against the Kelmendi family. Soon after that they were expelled from -- or we were expelled from Pristina and were no longer an authority there because the international forces an international community came in, so we as a court were no longer able to undertake any steps to uncover the perpetrators of that crime.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Nice, was the question you asked there that Mrs. Kelmendi said it was Serbs that took her husband?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: It was, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: It's just it's not recorded on the transcript.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: She had made it clear, didn't she, that it was Serbs that had taken her husband and sons?

utterances.speaker: DANICA MARINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: But she had no concrete proof of that --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I see.

utterances.speaker: DANICA MARINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- name and surname.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And --

utterances.speaker: DANICA MARINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: So that at the time when she said that, we still didn't know whether they were alive or not and where they were, what had happened to them.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Did you in your report put down anything that might indicate that it was the KLA that had killed the Kelmendis?

utterances.speaker: DANICA MARINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You know what? I couldn't introduce that into the minutes because I conduct the on-site investigation on the spot, take note of the situation I find on the ground. In my minutes and records I don't express my doubts or suspicions or observations and conclusions. I just describe what I find. I describe the location and the proof and evidence that I came upon in that location.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: DANICA MARINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: And that is all set out. I have the minutes or the record. I have it all, and the criminal report on that case and it is registered, so we as the court authorities took all the necessary steps to uncover the perpetrators of that crime. There is a criminal report. Along with a criminal report, we have the on-site investigation record, and so on.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... and I asked you whether you put down anything that indicated that the KLA had killed the Kelmendis. Is your answer that you did not do that?

utterances.speaker: DANICA MARINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not in my minutes, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: DANICA MARINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Because it is not up to me to write things like that down, observations of that nature.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: You raised issues last week or the week before, whenever it was, about the number of people killed and the names of people killed, your list being different in some particulars from the list in the indictment.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Your Honours, the position is that following that evidence, we've been able to make some headway in resolving differences on the lists. I'm going to deal with it, or Mr. Saxon will deal with it with the next witness, Dobricanin, and I'm not going to duplicate the position. Therefore, I have one general question to ask of this witness that I hope will clarify matters, or perhaps two.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Dealing with names, Mrs. Marinkovic, it is right that Kosovo Albanians often are known by more than one name? For example, somebody's last name may at some stage in his life change because he'll adopt the name of his grandfather.

utterances.speaker: DANICA MARINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know that that was the official position, that they changed names officially. I don't know about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: You lived there for a long time. Is it right that individuals could be known by more than one name? We can actually, I think, see it in your own documents but I just want a general answer to that. Is it right that individuals could be known by more than one name quite regularly?

utterances.speaker: DANICA MARINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They have a name and a surname. Now, I don't know whether they add their grandfather's name or not. It's not something I thought about nor did it influence my work, the establishment of this.
