If anybody wanted to change their name, they would need to do so officially and go about it officially, stating the reasons for wishing to change their names, and this is then recorded in the records, the books of married, dead, and so on. Yes, I have lived in Kosovo for a long time but this is not something that I know about for a fact.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Finally, or almost finally, just sweeping up matters of detail, I asked you at the beginning, or fairly early on, about your husband's first name and you having provided it. The Court will find him referred to in tab 5.1 of the Balevic exhibits. I'm not asking you to turn it up, but that's a reference. Because in fact your husband was sufficiently involved in local Serb politics that he was one of the speakers at the meeting attended by the accused at Kosovo Polje in '87, wasn't he, because we've got a transcript from a Defence exhibit of what he said. He spoke at that meeting, didn't he?

utterances.speaker: DANICA MARINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, he must have spoken, but he wasn't officially involved in politics as a politician. He's a mechanical engineer by profession. He worked as an engineer in a factory. And like all Serbs at the time who lived in Kosovo and Metohija, he -- or, rather, they sought their rights in Kosovo and Metohija because they were second-rate citizens at the time. At that time, the Albanians enjoyed much more rights --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... thinking back, he was actually on the committee with the man Solevic and others that organised the demonstrations around the country, wasn't he? He was actually on the committee.

utterances.speaker: DANICA MARINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I didn't quite understand that. What kind of demonstrations? I didn't understand that.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: When Serbs went from Kosovo to Vojvodina to bring down the Vojvodina then government, it was a committee organising it and your husband was one of the committee.

utterances.speaker: DANICA MARINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: What does that have to do with my testimony now? Secondly, they did not go out there to topple the Vojvodina government, to bring down the Vojvodina government. They wanted to portray how the Serbs in Kosovo and Metohija were endangered in so many ways. They didn't have the right to get jobs, because Albanians were given preference. They didn't have the right to get an apartment, and so on. The Serbs only raised their voice so that Serbia would hear that there were Serbs living in Kosovo and Metohija too and that they should have the same rights as Albanians. That was the aim of those demonstrations. It was aimed at that. But that has nothing to do with my work. I was a judge, I remain a judge, and I'm a judge even now after the new government came into place. I continue to work as a professional judge. What my husband did at the time by way of giving his contribution to improve the lot of Serbs in Kosovo and Metohija is something that really has nothing to do with my job. No one ever made any objections to the way I did my job, not from the side of the Prosecution or the Defence attorneys.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... Defence attorneys. Now, we only looked at one example and it took too long, but in fact several complaints were made about your -- please listen to me. Several complaints were made about your allowing or encouraging people to be beaten when detained. More than one in the very police case that we looked at, tab 4. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: DANICA MARINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is not correct. That was not a complaint of my work. It is only natural that a Defence attorney on behalf of his client has to write some kind of submissions. He did not have any objections to my work. He asked for his client to be examined, I allowed that, and that was the end of that. But during investigation --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: DANICA MARINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- it defies all logic that I could force someone to give his signature and give an admission. I don't believe that a judge could work that way anywhere in the world because the work of judges and the courts of law is exposed to the public and to appraisals by the public. The trial was public after the indictment was issued. So he could have said the same thing in his appeal. On the contrary. When you mentioned the illegal SUP --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... is that, as we saw from the limited nature of the inquiry at Racak, I must suggest to you that over the period of time, which is why we've looked at a longer period of time and indeed your husband's interest in politics as well as your own behaviour, I must suggest to you that over a period of time you were putting the law in the service of political objectives. You see?

utterances.speaker: DANICA MARINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is not correct. I have nothing to do with politics nor was I ever involved in politics. I have only worked professionally and in accordance with the law.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Your Honours, exhibits now or later? In your hands.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: I think later.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, do you have any re-examination?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreters did not hear the speaker.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: The interpreters did not hear -- hear me or Mr. Milosevic?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic. The microphone wasn't on.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You asked me whether I had any additional questions, and my answer was yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. Proceed. Proceed.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. Robinson.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mrs. Marinkovic, at the beginning of the cross-examination, Mr. Nice put questions that had to do with your credibility, and he showed a text written by Natasa Kandic, which in all fairness had not been translated, but very serious accusations were levelled at you. Therefore, I shall put a few questions -- let me just find something here. A few questions that have to do with that text. At the bottom of the first page, I'm saying that for the benefit of you who can follow the text in English, the paragraph begins as follows: "[In English] More and more policemen are coming out with what really happened in Kosovo. It was from them that I first heard about the murder of Fehmi Agani. I also heard from them that liquidation orders --" [Interpretation] please pay attention to this, Mrs. Marinkovic: "[In English] were not given only by police and military commanders." [Interpretation] Let's dwell on this sentence first. Have you ever heard of any police or military commander giving orders for any kind of liquidation?

utterances.speaker: DANICA MARINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've never heard of anything like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Now the next sentence: "[In English] They told me Danica Marinkovic personally ordered several wounded men of the Ahmeti family to be shot on 28 February 1998 in Likosane village." [Interpretation] As you can see, Mrs. Marinkovic, Natasa Kandic accused you here that you ordered the killing of a few members of the Ahmeti family. Please, do you know anything about what it says here?

utterances.speaker: DANICA MARINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Nothing. I was never there nor do I know anything in relation to this event. This is a pure lie, and it is totally untrue in relation to me as an individual and as a professional.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Is it conceivable at all that there would be a situation in which an investigating judge could issue any kind of action, especially something as serious as a killing?

utterances.speaker: DANICA MARINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is inconceivable. No one can order that. That kind of thing could never happen.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. Mrs. Marinkovic, are you saying that you've never been to the village of Likosane?

utterances.speaker: DANICA MARINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I've never been there. I don't even know if it fell under my jurisdiction.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. Then it says here: "[In English] Then an investigating judge, she came to conduct an on-site investigation together with Jovica Jovanovic, the deputy district prosecutor, and a team of investigators. There was a pile of bodies outside the Ahmeti house in which some men were still giving signs of life. In the presence of about 30 members of the special anti-terrorist unit, Danica Marinkovic allegedly said, 'I'm not taking them. Kill them.'"

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, may I remind you that the witness has already contradicted this statement. She has already denied the allegations in that statement. So I mean, there is no profit really from just having her reiterate her denial.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May I add something? This is the first time I see this text. This is the first time I've heard of this. I never had the opportunity of reading this before. I mean, something like this being written is really something that is beyond any reason. I'm so surprised that anybody could write something like this and that any newspaper would carry it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Please take a look at the fourth paragraph starting from the bottom. I'm going to read it out to you. Again your name is mentioned there. "[In English] Judge Marinkovic sets herself up as a protector of Serb victims and the Serbian police but here attempts to manipulate public opinion and in vain. It is known within the police force who killed Fehmi Agani, who did what in Kosovo, who fired the guns, who removed the corpses, who looted by the truckload, who brought the orders from Belgrade and conveyed the president's commendation and expressions of support." [Interpretation] Please, could you be so kind as to give your comment with regard to what I've just read out to you.

utterances.speaker: DANICA MARINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is also a lie. It is something that is untrue. It is a sheer invention. First of all, I carried out investigations regardless of whether who -- of who the victim was, whether it was a Serb, Albanian, or anybody else. When I go to an on-site investigation, I have no idea who the victim is. And I have such a lot of proof that I carried out all on-site investigations regardless of any kind of background. I mentioned a few minutes ago also as far as Fehmi Agani is concerned, I had nothing to do with him and I did not carry out the on-site investigation because this was a perpetrator unknown and also the body was first of an unknown person, so then I asked for a post-mortem to be carried out. A criminal report was filed against perpetrators unknown. That is to say that the state authorities, in accordance with their powers, did everything that could be done in relation to that event.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. In this same passage, it says that it was known full well "who brought the orders from Belgrade [In English] and conveyed the president's commendations and expressions of support."

utterances.speaker: DANICA MARINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That has nothing to do with anything. We had no links with Belgrade. We did our jobs professionally and in accordance with the law. It's not that any kind of communications or commendations arrived to the court, either to me personally or my colleagues or to the office of the prosecutor.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, we have another trial this afternoon, so in order to give them time to make the changeover, we're going to stop a few minutes before a quarter to two. We will adjourn and resume tomorrow morning at 9.00 a.m.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well, Mr. Robinson.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Thursday, the 7th day of April, 2005, at 9.00 a.m.

procedural_notes.text: --- Whereupon the hearing adjourned at 1.43 p.m.
